David Walliams' unprecedented legal battle not to be named in relation to allegations against him went downhill as he tried to secure a permanent injunction.

He was named by the Guardian and ITN because he had no sound legal reason to prevent the news organisations' investigation from being published. In response to the allegations included, Walliams said he was "not a sexual predator" and had not "broken the law".

The 55-year-old's bid for an injunction had been an open secret from the start after what would have normally been an anonymised application briefly appeared under his own name on a court cases register.

His exceptionally unusual attempt to gag the media - forever - became clear at the full trial last month - but that's when his bid to remain anonymous got worse.

In court, his lawyers did not claim that the investigation would be disclosing legally confidential or private information the journalists were not entitled to - two avenues often trod to silence reporters.

Instead lawyers for Walliams argued that such was the threat to his life from publication that the court itself would be breaching his human rights, were it to allow the story to go ahead.

This was, the court ultimately concluded, unheard of.

Under Article 2 of the European Convention on Human Rights, the British state has a duty to take reasonable steps to try to protect life where they can do so and, importantly, where a particular body has an actual responsibility to do so.

There's no expectation that a state agency can save all lives in all circumstances - but it must show it has done its best if it is clear it had a responsibility to act.

The most obvious example of this law in practice is that the police must try to act on credible intelligence of a threat to life, even if the intended victim is a gangster.

But that duty, and how it should be applied in the real world, is also why Walliams lost: he was expecting the wrong public body to be doing the protecting.

The High Court's Mr Justice Nicklin said that the responsibility to try to protect the comedian and author's life was on clinicians and the hospital he had already been taken to. He had been detained for his own protection, meaning the state was already trying to meet its obligation to protect him from harm.

The court could not do that protecting because it had not taken responsibility for Walliams' psychiatric treatment or safety. Its role was to decide the legal dispute between Walliams and the news organisations.

Walliams' lawyers had suggested that there might be a right to private family life issue in the case but the judge said there had been no evidence to detail that, and he had to take into account the media's right to freedom of speech to publish what was described in court as a detailed investigation in the public interest.

If the media were wrong about their claims, Walliams could later sue for defamation - the way that any party seeks redress against journalists who have published a story that’s untrue and highly damaging to their reputation.

After Walliams lost last week, and the court's judgment underlines how seriously it considered the risks to him to be, Mr Justice Nicklin asked whether there were plans for an appeal.

But Walliams had not been able to give his lawyers instructions on how to proceed.

"There is a degree of urgency - the court has moved exceptionally quickly to accommodate this trial and produce this judgment," said Mr Justice Nicklin. "It is slightly concerning that there is not an ability to proceed today. I don't understand really. If I was satisfied that there were compelling reasons why permission to appeal should be granted I could say so now. "

Sara Mansoori KC, Walliams' counsel, said the case raised "novel issues of law based on unusual facts" but because of the vulnerable nature of her client - in hospital - she needed more time.

The judge gave Walliams until 16:30 GMT on Monday to come up with some proper grounds to challenge his decision. Those papers were never filed.

The failure to launch an appeal bid meant that ITN and the Guardian were free to publish.

While all this had been going on in court - there was a social media-sized elephant in the room. No end of people were posting 'It's David Walliams' and wondering why we bona fide journalists were not saying the same.

When the courts in the UK order that someone should remain anonymous, that order applies to all forms of publishing and broadcasting. It matters not whether the publication is in a newspaper or online - it is still publication. That is why bona fide journalists who understand the law did not wade in.

But there is a massive practical issue: how far does the writ of English law run in cyber space?

One judge I recently addressed over a reporting restriction issue described social media as a "wild west". That comment underlines the concern among legal professionals.

But the question is how to enforce injunctions in an age of rapid fire digital gossip?

If a newsroom were to breach an order, the nature of a large media organisation's audience means that publication would be seen by judges to be rather grave and the editor would likely be up in court.

One random user of X publishing the suspected identity of an anonymised person by passing on gossip is obviously less impactful. If Chad from Utah reposts Dorothy from Liverpool's gossip, the chances of being hauled before a judge are even more remote.

But what happens when thousands of people are all saying the same - and then their claims, perhaps based on a kernel of unreportable truth, are magnified by AI summaries and algorithms dripping content into phones?

At that point, mathematically speaking the impact is greater than one single newsroom breaching an injunction.

The public's perception of the Walliams case was complicated because his name became known from the start - but the furious gossip over who "PPT" really was shows there is an existential threat to how courts try to control information to prevent harm. And it's not clear whether they have any answer to it.

Will Smallbone's strike proved to be the winner for Leicester City against Walsall

Brentford U21 and League One side Leicester City both moved into the knockout stages of the Jersey Mike's Trophy with vital victories.

The Bees had to beat the Football League's basement side Crawley Town in their final fixture in Southern Group H to progress and did so courtesy of a Domeiro Bobb-Semple double in a 2-1 success at Broadfield Stadium, where Connor Wickham scored on his Crawley debut.

In Southern Group B, the Foxes trailed at the King Power Stadium against League Two Walsall, who would have gone through in place of their hosts with a win. But strikes from Will Smallbone and John Lundstram put them ahead by the break and they held on.

Stevenage topped the group by beating Fulham U21 on penalties.

Chelsea U21 were not in action but went through at the expense of Reading , who needed a big win away against Bristol Rovers to see them overtake the west London side in Southern Group C, but the Royals were beaten on penalties.

Nottingham Forest U21 and Notts County both eased through into the last 16 with wins in Northern Group F.

Forest enjoyed a 3-0 success against League Two promotion-chasers Grimsby Town at Blundell Park, where all the goals came before the break.

The Magpies moved into the knockout stages as group winners by beating League One Burton Albion by the same scoreline for a third win in three EFL Trophy games.

Domeiro Bobb-Semple (right) scored a goal in each half for the Bees youngsters

In Southern Group F, Leyton Orient needed a big victory over Barnet to claim an unlikely second-placed finish on goal difference, but they were well beaten at The Hive, with Jack Maskell's first-half strike setting the hosts on the way to a 4-2 win.

Oxford United coasted to a 4-0 win over Cheltenham Town to go second in Southern Group A - and will stay there as long as they avoid a heavy defeat against Tottenham Hotspur U21 in their final fixture.

In Southern Group G, Gillingham made sure of their place in the last 32 by seeing off Northampton Town 2-1. The Gills only needed a point to be certain of finishing in second place above Brighton & Hove Albion U21, but Lamin Sillah scored one goal and made another to inspire his side to victory over their League Two rivals.

Seb Campbell crashed home a 99th-minute winner as Plymouth Argyle beat Swindon Town at Home Park to finish top of the pile in Southern Group E, while Colchester United beat Ipswich Town U21 on penalties after a 0-0 draw in Southern Group D, in a match where both sides knew their campaign had ended after their second fixture.

Elsewhere, a close-range shot by Tom Graves put Crewe Alexandra on track for the win they needed to progress from Northern Group B, but Wigan Athletic scored twice in the second half to dash their hopes, while veteran forward Nick Powell was among the scorers as Bradford City thumped York City 4-0 to top Northern Group C.

In a thriller in Northern Group D, already eliminated Mansfield Town looked set for their first points of the competition as they led already qualified Chesterfield 3-1 with 28 minutes remaining. But Dylan Duffy scored two of four goals in the closing stages to earn the Spireites a remarkable 5-3 victory.

Stockport County beat Tranmere Rovers on penalties in Northern Group E, but both sides were already sure of qualification, while Huddersfield Town thumped Liverpool U21 4-0 to finish top of Northern Group H.

Paige Tomlinson from Barnsley loves the "chilled" lifestyle of Cairns in northern Australia

In a Mexican restaurant in north-east Australia, the tacos are served by staff from France, Italy, Ireland and Argentina.

Cairns has long attracted a young and transient international crowd, who enjoy the tropical lifestyle while earning money for travel.

But one nationality is in shorter supply than it used to be.

"You get far fewer British backpackers looking for jobs here these days," says Mexicairns owner Peter McLeay.

It's a trend McLeay has noticed since mid-2023, when a free trade deal between the UK and Australia kicked in.

That agreement - as well as tariff-free trade in Tim Tams and Penguins - included special treatment for Brits on working holiday visas: exemption from having to find jobs in regional or remote places if they wanted to remain beyond a year.

That, along with an increase in the age limit from 30 to 35 saw backpacker visas issued to Brits surging from 47,200 in 2023-24 to just over 77,000 in 2025-26, according to the latest Australian government data.

Without the incentive to go regional, many are choosing to base themselves in the big cities, or, according to Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, "Bondi or Coogee" - two of Sydney's most famous beachside suburbs.

Now though, with Brits making up almost a quarter of all 323,000 backpacker visas issued last year, his government wants the free trade deal to be revisited.

Many British backpackers end up in Bondi, PM Anthony Albanese says, instead of exploring the rest of Australia

"Many Brits don't treat it as a working holiday anymore. It's more a three-year career break," says Dan McConnell, general manager of the Mad Monkey backpacker hostel chain.

He says Brits used to be the largest clientele at its Cairns accommodation but "now French outnumber British three to one".

"We see the Brits get to Sydney, decide it's the coolest place in the world, and stay there," he adds.

It's a privilege not enjoyed by working holidaymakers from other countries who must do at least 88 days of "specified regional work" in industries that need a seasonal or temporary workforce - including agriculture, fisheries, tourism and hospitality - if they want to qualify for a second year extension, and six months to stay a third year.

Barely a month ago, Albanese ruled out forcing British backpackers to do the same, accepting it as part of the trade deal.

But, under pressure from businesses here in Far North Queensland and other regional Australian communities, who are concerned about a lack of labour, the mood music has changed.

Last week Albanese met UK counterpart Andy Burnham at the meeting of Commonwealth leaders in the Caribbean.

And alongside AI, gender violence online and the AUKUS defence pact, backpackers were on the agenda.

Despite speculation in the Australian media, no immediate announcement was made. Albanese instead told reporters that he had pushed for a change in the rules on backpackers and that Burnham had been "very constructive about it".

"We'll work those issues through over coming weeks," he said adding that the free trade agreement was not set in stone and tweaks could be made "if there are good policy reasons".

Backpackers make up one in seven farm jobs across Australia, with about 52,000 people on working holiday visas doing jobs in horticulture each year, according to the National Farmers Federation.

It welcomed Albanese's discussions with Burnham, but said the issue of worker shortages in agriculture was far broader than the UK deal.

Of greater concern are wider proposals, announced in September, to cut net migration into Australia, under political pressure from the resurgent right wing populist One Nation party and the opposition coalition.

That includes an overhaul of the working holiday visa system, introducing a ballot for backpackers wanting to extend their stay – capped at 45,000 for people wanting a second year in Australia (down from 57,000 who qualified this year) and just 5,000 allowed to remain for a third year (compared with 31,000 this year).

This, the federation says, is "a low blow".

Those plans are still out for consultation, but immigration officials have slowed processing rates for some working holiday visa applications and paused them from several countries.

Tourism Tropical North Queensland chief executive Mark Olsen has also been among those lobbying Albanese in Canberra - telling him that backpackers brought both the spending power and the temporary labour needed to fill seasonal roles in a region famed as a gateway to the Great Barrier Reef and the Unesco world heritage listed Daintree rainforest.

Young Brits temporarily living and working in this region peaked at around 20,000 he says. Now it's closer to 11,000.

"Numbers have dropped significantly since the UK free trade agreement kicked in when border arrangements returned to normal [after the pandemic] in 2023 ," he said.

Peter Inderbitzen (right) relies heavily on seasonal workers including backpackers at his farm in Queensland

Cairns restaurateur Fintan Rafferty says that of about 180 staff on his payroll across four venues, only five are British. Prior to the visa rule change, that was closer to 25.

UK workers came with good skills in hospitality and "were willing to work, and to work flexible hours", he told the BBC.

And, he said, it was a two-way street. "The pay is very good, the conditions are very good. And one of the great things about the 88-days rule is that it forces people to travel. It's enriching their experience."

Bucking the trend, at the bar of Gilligan's backpackers, Paige Tomlinson serves vodka and soda with plenty of ice and a broad South Yorkshire accent.

The 27-year-old, from Barnsley, has been in Cairns for four months, attracted by the "chilled" lifestyle and local waterfalls.

"Most people prefer Sydney and they question me all the time why I'm here," she laughs. "But I got to Sydney and I just didn't like it. It was too busy, too much like London and I don't like London."

She says she'd like to see the regional work requirement brought in for all Brits, "getting them out their comfort zone".

"If every other country's got to do it, why should we not?"

About 200km north, at Red Valley Farm in Lakeland, general manger Peter Inderbitzen agrees.

Workers mainly from Tonga, hired on a Pacific labour scheme, pick bananas there year-round.

But Inderbitzen also relies heavily on backpackers, especially at peak avocado season, employing about 25 people for a couple of months each year.

"It's very short, sharp, get it done, get it out kind of work," he told the BBC. "But without those pickers, the avos stay on the tree."

Ethan Phillips, 23, from Buckinghamshire says the new Australian proposals make sense

While a few British backpackers were still applying for work, numbers had "completely dropped off" since the rule change, said Inderbitzen, who'd "love" to see British travellers having an incentive to head to the regions.

"As much as it wasn't perfect, [that programme] was working."

Back in Cairns, most of the young Brits the BBC tracks down are on tourist visas - but many want to return for a working holiday.

Among them is Ethan Phillips, 23, from Buckinghamshire who has been having way too much fun to keep up to date with what politicians have been discussing.

"It makes sense for them to want us to do [regional work] again," he says. "I mean I'd rather not do it, but if we have to, it's only three months … it can't be that bad."

Thomas Markle appeared before a federal magistrate judge on Tuesday and was denied bond

Thomas Markle, the father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, is back in federal custody in Florida after allegedly removing his ankle monitor, according to court documents.

Markle appeared before a federal magistrate judge in the Florida city of Tampa on Tuesday and was denied bond. Prosecutors say he removed the monitor early that morning.

US Judge Lindsay S Griffin found on Tuesday that Markle had violated the conditions of his pretrial release, court documents show.

Markle, who has denied possessing images of child sex abuse, was arrested in Florida last week and placed under house detention. He was also ordered to wear a location monitoring device.

The BBC has contacted his representatives.

Griffin described Markle's housing situation as "untenable", writing in the order revoking his pretrial release that "based on the lack of suitable housing, no condition or combination of conditions would reasonably assure the safety of any other person or the community and the defendant's appearance in court".

He also ordered a medical evaluation for Markle and said he "must receive all necessary and prescribed medication unless discontinued by a physician".

"Release conditions are court orders, not suggestions," Bill Essayli, the US attorney for Central California, wrote on X on Tuesday.

"We will continue to prosecute this case to the fullest extent of the law," he added.

Markle, 82, was first arrested last week after the FBI, acting on warrants, searched storage units in Los Angeles registered to him which he had rented since 2008, with the last payment being made in October this year, the DoJ said.

Inside the units the FBI says agents seized about 78 items, including film negatives, slides and books that they allege contained child sex abuse material.

Witnesses "positively identified" Markle in two of the images believed to contain child sex abuse material.

In those images, the man pictured "appears to be in the age range of 30s to 40s", which suggests the alleged abuse dates back decades as Markle is currently 82 years old.

Markle appeared in court last week following his arrest. No plea was taken during the appearance, which set several conditions for his pretrial release, including that he be kept in home detention.

He is charged with one count of possessing indecent images of children, according to the DoJ.

FBI director Kash Patel said last week that Markle "allegedly targeted innocent children and sought to steal their innocence through his criminal actions".

Markle has called the allegations "sick lies".

He moved to the Philippines last year after he had a series of strokes, and lived in Cebu until May. He was reportedly learning to walk again in Florida after having his leg amputated.

The duchess has been estranged from her father since 2018. The BBC understands she broke contact with him last year, telling him she and the authorities knew he had abused young girls.

In a previously shared statement, Meghan confirmed the existence of the letter and wrote: "I am deeply distressed... my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed."

She said she hoped it could be understood why she had largely cut off contact from her father and did "not allow him to have contact with our children".

Sebastien Pocognoli is enjoying his return to Scotland training

Sebastien Pocognoli is delighted to welcome "exciting" Scott McTominay into his squad, saying the Napoli midfielder is one of the "fantastic leaders" that helped persuade him to become Scotland head coach.

The Belgian revealed the fit-again 29-year-old "is in my captain group of five" who will be relied upon to make sure his instructions are carried out on the field of play.

McTominay missed Pocognoli's first, four-game Uefa Nations League camp in charge as Scotland drew with Slovenia, lost to Switzerland, beat North Macedonia but then lost the return at home to the Slovenians.

The midfielder, who is back playing after a minor heart procedure, has revealed he received treatment to correct an irregular heartbeat two days before Scotland's World Cup win over Haiti in June.

"I don't have to paint a picture of how important a player he is for us," Pocognoli said as he prepared for Friday's meeting with North Macedonia at Hampden.

"He is exciting. He had a smile on his face from the minute he arrived at the camp."

Pocognoli added a strong leadership group helped him guide Union Saint-Gilloise to their first Belgian title in 90 years.

"Without leaders, you can't win anything," he said. "You need guys who are helping the staff bring the standard.

"We are really lucky that we have a lot of captains in this team.

"It is one of the reasons why I feel comfortable to come to Scotland as the gaffer because I know we have fantastic leaders who are committed to doing their best for their country."

Another of those is obviously captain Andy Robertson and Pocognoli said "it is fantastic" the Tottenham Hotspur left-back is set to equal Kenny Dalglish's record of 102 caps.

"We are really lucky in modern football to have a leader like him," he said.

Pocognoli has remained positive despite Scotland sitting third in Nations League Group B1 behind Switzerland and Slovenia and in danger of missing out on promotion.

He also learned a lot from each of his first four games in charge.

"We know what we need to improve, but it is always a short period of time - two days to prepare for the game," Pocognoli said.

Scotland need at least four points from their final two games to have a chance of a promotion play-off place.

Fail to get through and, depending on the draw, these next two games will be their last time together before the European Championship qualifiers.

"These two games, if we start the qualification in March, are the last package of games and we have to use it to be ready for the March camp," he added.

"If it is June, we have more time to prepare with friendlies. This camp is crucial for me in demanding the players try to impress me and do everything to improve."

MN202611_161btng4q4a.t:
Spain's King Felipe VI and Queen Letizia were greeted by bishops as they arrived at the funeral mass on Tuesday

Spain's King Felipe and Queen Letizia were among those who have attended a memorial service in tribute to the 69 victims of last month's deadly train crash.

The accident occurred when one train, travelling at high speed, ploughed into the back of another that was stationary on the Madrid-Seville line, near the small town of Urda, about 40 miles from Toledo.

It was the worst rail tragedy in Spain since 2013. Twenty-eight people remain in hospital.

"The tragic accident in Urda has left our families, our towns and our society with a pain that is difficult to accept," Archbishop Cerro Chaves told those present.

Representatives of those killed carried lit candles to the front of the cathedral and placed them next to the main altar. The first reading of the service was by Ana Benítez, sister of David Benítez, a 38-year-old father-of-two who died.

The king and queen were met with applause by bystanders as they entered the cathedral and at the end of the service, after Catholic Mass, they spoke to relatives of the victims.

Senior politicians also attended the service, including the leader of the opposition People's Party, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, the president of the Castilla-La Mancha region, Emiliano García-Page, and Transport and Economy Minister Carlos Cuerpo.

Cuerpo took on the transport portfolio following the resignation last week of Óscar Puente from the post.

The Archbishop of Toledo officiated the memorial service

Puente had come under mounting pressure following the crash, Spain's second major rail tragedy this year after 46 people died in a collision on the same high-speed line in January.

Some local people from the town of Adamuz in Andalusia, where that accident happened, as well as residents of Urda, were present for the memorial service.

The investigation into the recent accident is still in progress. Puente suggested that human error combined with a glitch in the safety system may have been the cause.

The tragedy happened a month before the 29 November general election and is seen as likely to hurt Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez's attempts to secure re-election.

The ceremony took place on the same day as a nationwide strike by train drivers, who are demanding greater safety on the rail network.

Rail services were also expected to be affected across the country on Wednesday due to a general strike, led by housing activists calling for urgent measures to control rental costs.

A soldier in the US Army has been arrested on suspicion of spying for Russia, British counter-terror police have said.

The 41-year-old senior serviceman was arrested near Gloucester on Tuesday.

Counter Terrorism Policing London said the man had been arrested under section one and section three of the National Security Act 2023.

Section one of the Act relates to obtaining or disclosing protected information, while section three relates to assisting a foreign intelligence service.

As part of the investigation, officers are carrying out searches at two locations in Gloucestershire.

The BBC understands the soldier was based at Imjin Barracks in Innsworth, Gloucestershire. The barracks serve as the headquarters of Nato's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps (ARRC) , a strategic operational base for the alliance.

Counter Terrorism Policing said it was not linked to any other ongoing investigations.

FBI director Kash Patel said in a statement: "This important arrest involves allegations of espionage, which is of the utmost concern to the United States and our allies."

He added: "While this investigation is continuing, I want to send a clear message – this FBI has no tolerance for anyone who breaks their oath to the United States and whose actions endanger our national security and that of our partners."

Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans, from Counter Terrorism Policing London, described the arrest as "significant".

"The allegations are serious and our investigation is very much ongoing," she said.

The unnamed soldier is currently in custody at a London police station.

He has been detained under the National Security Act 2023, allowing police to hold him without charge for up to 14 days.

Brig Gen Sean Stinchon, commanding general of US Army Counterintelligence Command, said: "The alleged conduct of a senior soldier, entrusted with sensitive information, is a sobering reminder that insider threats are real and persistent.

"I encourage anyone who thinks they've witnessed something suspicious to report it to their local counterintelligence office."

Additional reporting by Daniel Sandford, UK correspondent.

MN202611_oqhtlsaq2m.t:
Lilly Creightmore, who alleges Walliams groomed her as a teen, said she was angry at his behaviour

ITV News and the Guardian have published reports alleging that David Walliams has been accused of sexual misconduct by several women, including one who was aged 15.

The allegations were made as a part of a joint three-year investigation , external by the two news organisations, which was published after the entertainer lost a legal bid to stop the claims against him being made public.

Some of the women accuse Walliams of "grooming" them when they were teenagers. One now characterises her alleged encounter with Walliams at 15 years old as a "sexual assault".

In a letter to journalists published by the Guardian, Walliams said he was "not a sexual predator" and had not "broken the law".

He said he "realised that at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with" and said he regretted not always taking "people's feelings properly into account".

If you are affected by any of the issues in this story, help and support is available at BBC Action Line.

Walliams shot to fame alongside Matt Lucas in the early 2000s with BBC sketch comedy Little Britain, and also served as a judge on ITV's Britain's Got Talent and launched a best-selling series of children's books.

The Guardian and ITV News say that several of the women, who do not know one another, allege they were targets of unwanted sexual advances from Walliams.

One woman alleges she met Walliams at a fan event when she was 15. She says he groomed her and they had sex when she was 17

Another woman alleges she met Walliams for a coffee when she was 15, before going back to his house where he allegedly tried to lift up her shirt and commit an act that she now describes as a sexual assault

A woman who worked as a model in her teens accused Walliams of grooming her. A different woman who also worked as a model said Walliams tried to kiss her while showing her around his home

The investigation claimed Walliams had a sexual relationship with at least one junior employee at publisher HarperCollins, and pursued another

Other women allege inappropriate behaviour at ITV's Britain's Got Talent, such as inviting girls and young women to his dressing room

In a letter addressed to journalists working on the ITV and Guardian investigation, Walliams wrote: "Looking back, I realise that at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with.

"I realise I did not always take people's feelings properly into account. That is something I regret. And whilst a power imbalance is inevitable when one party is famous, abusing that power is something else entirely and it is something that I never did."

He added: "I am not a sexual predator. I have not broken the law, but I am devastated that some of the women I met 10 to 20 years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me."

After the investigation was published on Tuesday, Walliams's long-time literary agent Independent Talent Group confirmed it had dropped him.

A BBC spokesperson described the allegations as "serious" and the corporation has removed Little Britain from BBC iPlayer.

Sky also described the allegations as "extremely serious", saying it was dropping its upcoming adaptation of Walliams's fantasy feature Fing! and had "already removed content which features him from our platforms".

The Metropolitan Police said it has contacted the Guardian and ITV News to "to ensure that any potential victims" are "made aware of how they could report any criminal allegations to police".

Walliams (right, with Matt Lucas, in 2006) shot to fame on the BBC comedy sketch series Little Britain

One of the women who alleged Walliams "groomed" her as a teenager told BBC Newsnight she was "angry" at his behaviour.

Lilly Creightmore - who Walliams contacted when she was 18 - waived her right to anonymity.

Creightmore told Newsnight that a month after they first met, Walliams told her she "could move in with him and basically that I could be his flatmate".

She said that after she arrived to stay at his house she "felt instantly pressured to share a bed with him".

"In the evenings, he would sort of come and sit with me and stroke my leg, and one night I think he put his head in my lap and sort of be like, 'are you sure you don't want to come and sleep in my bed with me?' I had an inner strength like, 'no I'm not attracted to you in that way'... I felt I was being manipulated," she added.

She told Newsnight: "I am angry, I'm suppressing it well, but just that this culture of older men in positions of power needs to go, needs to stop. They're abusing their positions, using young people and abusing young people, and people of any age of course. There were too many men in power still, that are doing this and they need to go."

Walliams's lawyers told the ITV News and Guardian investigation that he denied grooming Creightmore or acting inappropriately. They added he did not "target" her because she was "vulnerable" or "young".

Walliams said he believed his friendship with Lilly was a "special one" and felt "devastated" by her account. He denied the offers of help or gifts were attempts to groom, manipulate or coerce her into sleeping with him.

Two women, given pseudonyms of Alex and Jade in the investigation, have alleged that they first had contact with Walliams when they were 15 years old.

Alex alleged that she met Walliams in 2004 at a fan event when she was 15. She claimed that she and Walliams stayed in touch over the next two years and they had consensual sex for the first time when she was 17, the report alleged.

'I think I was groomed, 100%' David Walliams accuser tells ITV News

Asked how she feels about Walliams now, she told the investigation: "I think I was groomed. 100%."

Walliams told the publications he believed she was 18 at the time they had sex. The investigation said Alex had joked to Walliams in an email she was "old enough to go drinking", but was actually 17.

Walliams denied grooming Alex. He said he is "mortified to learn" that their "brief, consensual relationship has caused her sadness".

Jade also alleged she met Walliams when she was 15, in August 2007, in a Soho cafe.

Later, at his home, she alleged, he kissed her, lifted up her T-shirt, went on to commit an act that she now characterises as a sexual assault, and tried to put her hand down his trousers. She referred to what happened that night as "unwanted physical touching and emotional manipulation".

She said she considers what she says happened to her to have been "grooming", adding: "It's completely wrong in every way."

Walliams strongly denied that he had any sexual contact with Jade. He said he rejected any allegations of criminal activity and says he has never engaged in the grooming of young women.

Another woman, named as Ella, says she was 19 and working as a model when she rejected Walliams when he tried to kiss her during a tour of his home.

She referred to what happened that night as "unwanted physical touching and emotional manipulation".

Walliams said he made a "clumsy pass" at Ella, and he made no further approaches. He said he had no intention of intimidating Ella, or making her feel uncomfortable.

Other women claimed they were invited to Walliams's dressing room at Britain's Got Talent, or contacted by him after attending a taping.

Walliams (centre, in 2019) served as a judge for 10 series of ITV's Britain's Got Talent

Syco Entertainment, the company that created Britain's Got Talent, said it had had "no knowledge of the allegations described and was not made aware of them at the time".

The show's production company, Fremantle UK, said "no complaint has ever been made" against Walliams and encouraged anyone who "feels they have been the subject of any impropriety or wrongdoing by anyone... to come forward".

Women who worked for publisher HarperCollins also allege Walliams behaved inappropriately towards younger female employees.

One intern at the company told colleagues she had had a consensual sexual relationship with Walliams, but felt it was an "abuse of power".

After conducting an internal investigation, HarperCollins announced it was dropping Walliams as an author. Earlier this year, it also said it would no longer be publishing his back catalogue.

In a statement responding to ITV News and the Guardian's investigation, the company said it takes employee wellbeing "extremely seriously".

Walliams denies that he sexually harassed anyone at HarperCollins or behaved inappropriately in the workplace.

Walliams, 55, previously brought legal action against Independent Television News (ITN), which makes ITV News, and Guardian News and Media (GNM), publisher of the Guardian, to try and prevent the claims being published.

The two news organisations had argued that they believed it was in the public interest to publish the allegations.

Walliams denied the claims and his lawyers said any publication would be "highly likely" to lead him to kill himself, after two previous suicide attempts, and that the court should prevent any publication or broadcast.

Last week, a High Court judge rejected the injunction request and Walliams did not lodge an appeal, clearing the way for him to be named.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has become the face of the US AI boom

Nvidia has hired one of the largest law firms in the US to investigate the affair between its own chief executive and an alleged Chinese spy.

Jensen Huang, who co-founded the tech company, has admitted to having a romantic relationship outside of his marriage. The woman, Alice Huang, is alleged to be a spy for Beijing.

Nvidia said on Tuesday that it had hired New York law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz, and that its attorney Joon Kim would lead "a thorough and independent investigation". The FBI is also conducting its own probe .

The company's share price has fallen almost to a yearly low, with $500bn (£375bn) wiped of its stock market value since Friday.

Nvidia is widely considered one of the most important companies behind the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, given it is the sole manufacturer of a computer chip used in AI tools.

It is the world's second most valuable company after Apple and its chips have become a matter of national security for US officials who are keen to win the AI race.

Alice Huang, who is also known as Huang Le, and is not related to Jensen Huang, was an executive at Singaporean company Megaspeed, which has been a customer of Nvidia.

Megaspeed had been suspected of helping divert Nvidia chips to China, a concern that Nvidia has said was investigated and debunked.

Nvidia has also maintained that the US government did not inform it that Megaspeed posed an intelligence concern.

What we know so far about Jensen Huang's affair with suspected Chinese spy

Zoe Kleinman: Nvidia CEO's affair will cause ripples across US and beyond

According to the New York Times, Secretary of State Marco Rubio sent a memo to top officials in Washington earlier this year warning that Jensen Huang was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy.

Beijing has rejected claims that the Nvidia chief has been targeted, with its foreign ministry saying the allegations were "intended to smear and malign China".

US President Donald Trump said on Monday that he had spoken to Jensen Huang, who had said he had "no idea she was a spy." Trump said he believed him.

However, the relationship has drawn more political attention. Congressional leaders of the House Committee on Foreign Affairs have asked Huang to appear next week for a closed door briefing.

The Nvidia boss has yet to say whether he will attend, a person familiar with the committee's demand told the BBC. The committee has the authority to subpoena Huang, effectively forcing him to appear before it, if deemed necessary.

When announcing on Sunday that it would investigate the affair, Nvidia's board said it had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised.

It added that a committee of independent directors would oversee the probe.

Watch: Who is suspected Chinese spy at centre of Nvidia affair investigation?

Wachtell is one of the largest law firms in the US and has several notable clients in the tech industry. Among them are OpenAI and Salesforce.

Joon Kim is a former US Attorney for New York's Southern District and spent several years working as a government attorney focusing on fraud and other criminal acts.

The Nvidia investigation will likely be treated as urgent, according to sources familiar with the matter, as Jensen Huang's public image is tightly intertwined with the company.

He has become a key public figure in the development on AI, arguing the technology is a "new industrial revolution" and is on par with the advent of electricity.

It is unclear, however, if Wachtell will be able to interview Alice Huang.

A spokesperson for Nvidia declined to comment on Tuesday when asked if Jensen Huang had retained any of his own legal representation amid the company investigation and the separate one launched by the FBI.

Protesters have lit fires in the middle of roads

Police in Bangladesh have fired tear gas and rubber bullets to disperse supporters of the deposed Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, who are demanding her return to the country.

A police vehicle was set on fire in Gopalganj district, where the banned student wing of Hasina's Awami League party clashed with security forces.

Nationwide protests by pro-Hasina activists started a day after the former leader said she had requested a passport to return to Bangladesh from exile in India.

The demonstrations by the student wing, called Bangladesh Chhatra League (BCL), are seen as the first organised show of force by Hasina's supporters since she was ousted in August 2024 following a huge uprising against her rule .

Sheikh Hasina was ousted in 2024 following weeks of mass protests

Traffic was disrupted in some parts of the country as protesters tried to set up roadblocks using burning tyres.

Several passenger vehicles were also set on fire in various parts of Bangladesh in the run up to the protest.

A 60-year-old driver of a passenger bus was killed by smoke inhalation after people set fire to the vehicle in the city of Faridpur early on Tuesday.

Elsewhere, about 200 protesters briefly blocked traffic on the 6.2km (4 mile)-long Padma bridge across the Ganges, that connects the capital Dhaka with the south-western region.

Bangladeshi local media said dozens of crude bombs exploded in the past few days in Dhaka and elsewhere.

"Any attempt to worsen the law-and-order situation or create instability through any conspiracy within the country from across the border (India) will not be allowed to succeed," Bangladesh Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed said.

"Our supporters were not responsible for the violent incidents. They were carried out by unknown miscreants. We believe in peaceful protests," a senior leader of the BCL, who is now in exile in a foreign country, said.

Hasina fled to neighbouring India two years ago following a massive uprising, bringing an end to her 15-year reign.

Opposition parties accused Hasina of jailing political rivals, supressing dissent and overseeing widespread human rights abuses. She always denied the charges.

Student-led demonstrations against job quotas escalated into mass protests in 2024 after a bloody police crackdown

The United Nations has estimated up to 1,400 people were killed , most by gunfire from security forces, during the anti-government protests in 2024.

The activities of the Awami League were banned soon after she fled the country and it was not allowed to contest the February general election.

A special Bangladeshi tribunal last year sentenced her to death in absentia after being found guilty of crimes against humanity.

She has denied all the charges, calling the trial "biased and politically motivated".

Despite the death penalty threat, Hasina said she wanted to return to Bangladesh in December and requesteded the Bangladesh High Commission in New Delhi to issue her with a passport.

But the Bangladeshi government said the country would not provide a passport to her and called her "a terrorist".

"She is a fugitive criminal. We have an active extradition treaty with India. We want her handed over," Humaiun Kobir, Bangladesh's junior foreign affairs minister, said.

"Should we treat her like an ordinary commercial traveller and tell her to come and visit her in-laws' residence?" Kobir asked.

A state prosecutor in Bangladesh on Tuesday said the verdict would be executed if she came back, saying she had missed the opportunity to appeal.

Awami League leaders allege that in the past two years hundreds of supporters have been killed in mob violence and dozens have died in the custody of security forces.

Dhaka officials reject accusations that Awami League supporters are being systematically targeted.

A health visitor strike saw thousands of appointments cancelled

Health visitors are set to return to work next week after a deal was reached to end a nine-month strike that saw thousands of missed appointments.

Unite union said the agreement with Cwm Taf Morgannwg University Health Board would see all health visitors offered new roles, describing it as a "historic pay win" and a major victory for workers.

The health board said it had agreed to develop a new specialist health visitor role with additional responsibilities, subject to approval processes.

The Welsh government welcomed the return of staff and said that restoring services for babies and young children was now the priority.

About 100 health visitors with the health board have been on strike since February in a row over job grading, saying they were losing up to £9,000 a year as a result.

Home visits dropped dramatically, with the health board saying that safety and accessibility of services was its priority during the strike.

Between March and May 2025, the board, which covers Bridgend county, Merthyr Tydfil and Rhondda Cynon Taf, carried out 6,140 visits.

That dropped to 909 in the same period in 2026.

Unite general secretary Sharon Graham said the agreement was "a magnificent victory" for health visitors.

"This dispute was about recognising the skilled, vital work health visitors do for families and children in their communities," she said.

"Today that recognition has been secured."

Health board chief executive Paul Mears welcomed the resolution and said the immediate priority was restoring services for families.

He said a new specialist health visitor role would strengthen services and help the health board respond to local needs while recognising concerns raised by Unite on behalf of its members.

Plaid Cymru Senedd members representing constituencies across the health board area said they were "very relieved" health visitors were set to return to work and welcomed an outcome that delivered on promises made to staff.

In a joint statement, they said the dispute had highlighted the increasingly demanding role of health visitors and called on the health board to rebuild relationships with its workforce while tackling backlogs affecting families.

The Welsh government said it welcomed the return of health visitors to work and a route towards resolving the long-running dispute.

A spokesperson said health visitors provided vital support to children and families, including an important safeguarding role, and that the priority was now restoring services affected by the strike.

The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) told makers of popular weight-loss GLP-1 drugs that they must add warning labels about a rare eye condition that can cause sudden blindness.

Manufacturers of Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro and Zepbound must warn about nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION). The disorder happens when vessels supplying blood to the optic nerves become blocked, depriving the nerves of oxygen.

The condition can cause painless decreased vision in one eye, which can be permanent, the FDA said.

In a statement to the BBC, the American Academy of Ophthalmology said "any added risk appears small, and it has not been established that these medications cause NAION".

"GLP-1 medications offer important benefits for people with diabetes, obesity, and heart disease, so our message to patients is simple," the group said. "Don't stop your medication without talking to your doctor, and if you notice sudden, painless vision loss in one eye, see an ophthalmologist promptly."

There is no known treatment to reverse vision loss caused by NAION. It is the most common cause of acute optic nerve injury in people over 50 years old, according to the academy.

The FDA said it conducted a detailed review of reports of NAION in GLP-1 users as well as a review of other studies and concluded there is an "increased risk of rare NAION events" in people taking the drugs.

In a statement, Novo Nordisk, the manufacturer of Wegovy, one of the most popular weight-loss medications, said the company believes the data "do not establish a cause-and-effect relationship".

"We recognize that NAION can have a profound impact on patients and their families. Patient safety is a top priority for Novo, and we continue to monitor the safety of our medicines," the manufacturer said.

Some research was challenging to review because people taking GLP-1 drugs for obesity and type 2 diabetes may already have risk factors for NAION separate from the drugs, according to the regulator. The FDA said it was not known why those taking GLP-1 drugs may be more at risk for the eye condition.

The drugs already have warning labels for several other conditions including pancreatitis and gallbladder disease. Some of the most common symptoms for semaglutide - a key ingredient in many GLP-1 drugs - include nausea, vomiting and stomach pain.

⁠Last year, a safety arm of the European Medicines Agency, a part of the European Union, said up to 1 in 10,000 people taking semaglutide may be affected by NAION.

In a study published two years ago analysing 17,000 patients, US researchers found those taking semaglutide were four times more likely to be diagnosed with NAION than those not taking the drug.

But one of the authors of the study, Harvard Medical School ophthalmology professor Dr Joseph Rizzo, said the findings were "significant but tentative", and more research was needed on the relationship between the drug and the eye condition in a more diverse population.

The BBC's Jonathan Beale reported from inside Slovyansk, one of four cities that make up Ukraine's "fortress belt" - a system of heavily reinforced defence lines in the parts of eastern region of Donetsk still under its control.

The town has become almost uninhabitable and has been under heavy bombardment from Russian drones, missiles and glide bombs.

Members of a Ukrainian drone unit that call themselves Peaky Blinders, named after the cult BBC TV series, have taken on the task of intercepting Russian drones.

Russia wants Kyiv to give up the fortress cities and they are central to talks on a possible peace deal that have resumed after nine months between Ukraine, Russia and the US in Abu Dhabi.

MN202611_1j1ehvr7ecl.t:
Najib smiles to reporters at the Kuala Lumpur High Court after it cleared the way for him to go home

Malaysia's disgraced former Prime Minister Najib Razak has arrived home to begin serving the rest of a jail sentence for corruption under house arrest.

There was a big media presence at his Kuala Lumpur residence to see the 73-year-old return from prison in an SUV late on Tuesday night, escorted by a heavily armed police convoy.

Najib's return ended a four-year prison stint after he was found guilty over the embezzlement of billions of dollars from the country's sovereign wealth fund.

The 1MDB scandal brought down his government and made headlines around the world when it came to light a decade ago, embroiling prominent figures from Malaysia to Goldman Sachs and Hollywood.

Investigators estimated that $4.5bn (£3.3bn) was siphoned from the state-owned wealth fund, which Najib co-founded, into private pockets, including his own. More than $1bn allegedly ended up in accounts linked to Najib, according to prosecutors.

Najib's lawyers claim he had been misled by his advisers - in particular the financier Jho Low, who has maintained his innocence and remains at large.

Journalists jostled for a glimpse of Najib as he was driven to his home, which has been declared a federal prison

Najib's mansion in one of the capital's most exclusive neighbourhoods was declared a federal prison ahead of his homecoming on Tuesday.

Critics said his release from jail undermined efforts to fight corruption and questioned its legal basis, saying Malaysian law made no provision for house arrest.

Najib, who was prime minister from 2009 to 2018, denied wrongdoing but was convicted at two separate trials.

In the first trial he was sentenced in 2020 to 12 years in prison and jailed in 2022. The term was later halved on appeal.

In September, the King of Malaysia granted him a conditional pardon to see out the remaining two years of his sentence at home.

The transfer to his mansion was to take place on Friday but put on hold after the attorney general sought clarification of the royal decree. On Tuesday the high court ruled the house arrest was effective immediately.

Najib's party paid a $12m fine as part of the terms of the royal pardon allowing him to serve the rest of his term at home.

He was sentenced after being convicted of abuse of power, money laundering and breach of trust over 42 million ringgit ($10m; £7.7m) transferred from SRC International - a former unit of 1MDB - into his private accounts.

Najib is appealing against a 15-year prison sentence, handed down at a second trial in December 2025 , in a case involving much larger sums of money. In that case he was convicted of misappropriating nearly 2.3 billion Malaysian ringgit ($569m; £422m) from the nation's sovereign wealth fund 1Malaysia Development Berhad (1MDB).

He is due to start serving that sentence after his house arrest ends, which is expected in August 2028.

Umujyi wa Kigali n'uwa St. Louis ibarizwa muri Leta ya Missouri, imwe mu zigize Leta Zunze Ubumwe za Amerika, yasinyanye amasezerano y’ubufatanye azwi nka ‘Sister Cities Agreement’, agamije guteza imbere imikoranire mu bucuruzi, ishoramari, ubuhinzi, ikoranabuhanga, ubuvuzi, uburezi n’ibindi bikorwa by’iterambere.

Aya masezerano agamije guhuza ubushobozi n’ubunararibonye bw’imijyi yombi, hagamijwe kubyaza umusaruro amahirwe y’ubukungu, guteza imbere abaturage no gushimangira umubano hagati ya Kigali na St. Louis, yashyiriweho umukono i Kigali kuri uyu wa Kabiri tariki 10 Ugushyingo 2026.

Ni umuhango witabiriwe n’umuyobozi w’Umujyi wa Kigali wungirije ushinzwe Imiturire n’Ibikorwa remezo, Fulgence Dusabimana, Umuyobozi w’Umujyi wa St. Louis, Cara Spencer, hamwe n’Umuyobozi w’Intara ya St. Louis, Dr. Sam Page.

Nyuma yo gushyira umukono kuri aya masezerano Dusabimana yagaragaje ko u Rwanda rwashyizeho imirongo ihamye yorohereza ishoramari, irimo umutekano, icyerekezo cy’iterambere gisobanutse na politiki yorohereza abashoramari.

Yagize ati: “Ubufatanye bw’imijyi bubasha gupimwa neza si ku masezerano dusinye gusa, ahubwo ni ku mpinduka tuzana mu buzima bw’abaturage bacu.”

Yasobanuye ko Kigali yifuza ko aya masezerano azafasha ibigo by’ubucuruzi byo ku mpande zombi guhuzwa, abashoramari bagasurana, hakabaho imishinga ihuriweho, ihererekanya ry’ikoranabuhanga no gusangira ubumenyi.

Yanagaragaje ko hazashakishwa uburyo bwo guteza imbere imikoranire hagati ya za kaminuza, ibigo by’ubushakashatsi n’urubyiruko.

Umuyobozi w'Umujyi wa St. Louis, Cara Spencer, yavuze ko umubano w’imijyi yombi wubatswe mu gihe cy’imyaka myinshi ishize, ashimangira ko gusinya aya masezerano ari intangiriro y’ubufatanye bw’igihe kirekire.

Yashimye iterambere rya Kigali, by’umwihariko ibikorwa remezo, gahunda zishingiye ku iterambere ry’abaturage, ahantu hagenewe kugendwa n’amaguru n’ibikorwa ngarukakwezi bihuza ubuyobozi n’abaturage.

Uyu muyobozi yavuze ko umujyi ayoboye wa St. Louis ufite ubumenyi n’ubushobozi mu buhinzi, ubushakashatsi, ubuvuzi no guhanga udushya, bikaba bishobora gusangizwa u Rwanda.

Ati: “Turifuza ko St. Louis yaba ikiraro gihuza Kigali na Leta Zunze Ubumwe za Amerika, nk’uko u Rwanda ari irembo rya Afurika.”

Yongeyeho ko bazanye intumwa zigera kuri 40 zirimo abayobozi b’ibigo by’ubucuruzi n’abahagarariye inzego zitandukanye z’abaturage, bagamije gushaka amahirwe y’imikoranire mu Rwanda.

Umuyobozi w’Intara ya St. Louis, Dr. Sam Page, yagaragaje ko guhuza ubushobozi bw’iyo ntara n’ubukungu bw’u Rwanda burimo gutera imbere, bishobora kuvamo ishoramari n’imirimo mishya.

Ati: “Agaciro nyakuri k’ubufatanye bw’imijyi kaboneka iyo umubano urambye utagarukira muri za guverinoma gusa, ahubwo ugera no mu bigo by’ubucuruzi, mu mashuri, mu bigo by’umuco no mu baturage ubwabo.”

Impande zombi zemeranyije gushyigikira no guteza imbere imikoranire igirira akamaro impande zombi, hagamijwe kubaka imiyoboro mishya y’ubufatanye mu bukungu, binyuze mu bucuruzi n’ishoramari, hibandwa by’umwihariko ku buhinzi n’ikoranabuhanga rikoreshwa mu buhinzi, ubumenyi mu binyabuzima (biosciences), ubuvuzi, ikoranabuhanga mu itumanaho no guhanahana amakuru, igenamigambi ry’imijyi n’iterambere ry’ibikorwa remezo, kubungabunga ibidukikije no guteza imbere ubushobozi bw’abakozi.

Ubu bufatanye buzanibanda ku burezi n’amasomo ya za kaminuza, hamwe n’umuco, binyuze mu bigo bishinzwe siporo n’ubukerarugendo, abaturage b’imijyi yombi n’izindi nzego zizagaragazwa nk’izifite amahirwe y’imikoranire mu gihe kiri imbere.

Impande zombi kandi zanemeranyije gushyigikira no gushishikariza abaturage b’imijyi yombi gusurana, hagamijwe guteza imbere ubwo bufatanye no kubyaza umusaruro amahirwe azaboneka ku mpande zombi.

Umujyi wa St Louis waherukaga gusinya amasezerano nk’aya ya Sister Cities mu myaka 10 ishize, akaba ari na yo ya mbere Cara Spencer asinye kuva yaba umuyobozi w’uwo mujyi.

St. Louis, ni umujyi uherereye muri Leta ya Missouri, mu burengerazuba bwo hagati bwa Leta Zunze Ubumwe za Amerika (USA), ku nkombe z'uruzi rwa Mississippi ari narwo runini muri Amerika.

Uyu mujyi, uzwi cyane nk'umwe mu mijyi ifite ubukungu bushingiye ku buhanga mu buhinzi, ubuvuzi n'ubushakashatsi hamwe n'ikoranabuhanga n'inganda. Ukaba ufite umubare munini cyane w’abahanga mu bumenyi bw’ibimera kurusha ahandi ku isi.

Banafite ubukungu bwihuta mu bijyanye n’ibigo bishya by’ubucuruzi (startups). Ku bijyanye no koroshya ubwikorezi n’imitangire y’ibicuruzwa, aho uherereye hatanga amahirwe akomeye ku bashoramari baturutse i Kigali, mu Rwanda no muri Afurika muri rusange.

St. Louis kandi ni wo mujyi ubarizwamo Ikigo cy’Igihugu gishinzwe amakuru n’ikarita byifashisha amakuru y’ahantu (National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency – NGA), gifite uruhare mu bikorwa bijyanye na GPS no gukora amakarita arimo n’ay’inyanja.

Manchester United minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe (left), chief executive Omar Berrada (centre) and director of football Jason Wilcox will decide Michael Carrick's fate as head coach

Michael Carrick's future as Manchester United head coach will be determined 800 miles away from Old Trafford in Monaco on Wednesday.

Chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox are flying out for one of their regular pre-planned meetings to discuss strategy around the football club.

On this occasion, the main issue to be decided is Carrick's future and what should happen next.

It is expected that Berrada and Wilcox's recommendation is for the head coach to go.

The Red Devils have opened talks with USA head coach Mauricio Pochettino about replacing Carrick, should he be sacked.

It is not a situation Sir Jim Ratcliffe can have expected to find himself in again, less than three years after purchasing a minority stake in United.

On Christmas Eve 2023, his vision was much different.

"Our shared ambition is clear: we all want to see Manchester United back where we belong, at the very top of English, European and world football," he said.

Instead, United are 18th, in the Premier League's relegation zone after winning just one of their first 10 games and none since August. It is their lowest position so far into a top-flight season since 1986-87 when they were 20th.

Ratcliffe has been criticised for many decisions since he bought his 28.94% stake for just over £1bn. This is one he really needs to get right.

How close is Carrick to Man United exit?

Ratcliffe's home is in Monaco and his company Ineos has offices in the principality.

The meeting had been in the diary for some time as a regular catch-up between senior executives and their boss.

Sources have stressed that the choice of location was not influenced by the debate around Carrick's future - it just happens to now be the most important item for discussion.

The decision to sack United's previous two managers was not made in a meeting in Monaco.

Ruben Amorim was sacked 19 hours after his explosive media conference following a 1-1 draw at Leeds in January.

Erik ten Hag went a day after Manchester United lost at West Ham leaving them with just three wins from their opening nine matches

A decision to sack Dutchman Ten Hag was taken at a meeting of senior Ineos executives in the summer of 2024, only for the choice to be reversed following the FA Cup final triumph over Manchester City.

Four months later there was a six-hour meeting at Ineos HQ in London as Ten Hag's tenure hung by a thread. He survived again but was gone three weeks later.

Amorim was summoned to Monaco after the Europa League final defeat to Tottenham in 2025.

There is said to be daily communication between Berrada and Ratcliffe. So if the meeting was purely to decide Carrick's fate, it could be done by video conference, and the need to travel to Monaco is not the reason why there is yet to be a decision.

But the travel element does add a complication given Berrada and Wilcox want to inform Carrick of any decision first, and face to face.

Sources say the Monaco meetings used to be held every six weeks, although in more recent times they are less frequent.

Those who have attended them say they take place in the morning, tend to last between three and four hours and usually stop on time so Ratcliffe can go for his regular lunchtime jog.

Pochettino, Howe, Emery... or Carrick? Man Utd's managerial options

What Howe could bring to Man Utd - and what are the challenges?

Mauricio Pochettino was appointed USA boss in September 2024

United stood by Carrick after the woeful 3-0 home defeat by Bournemouth on 25 October.

Club sources were adamant they wanted to give Carrick and his players a chance to turn the situation around it was also felt that the two-week international break in November represented a better chance for the club to properly assess the club's start to the campaign.

However, although they did end a long wait for a victory against Roma on 3 November, United had to come from two goals down to seal a 3-2 victory in a chaotic game.

They failed to press home their advantage after excelling in the first half against Chelsea and eventually lost 2-0 as experienced central defender Lisandro Martinez was sent off.

On Sunday, they conceded twice inside five minutes and had to come from two goals down twice to claim a point against Villa.

While sources said the comebacks showed the United squad were still playing for Carrick, it is also understood the chaotic nature of the games and the inability to stop the opposition from scoring has led Berrada and Wilcox, who were at all three matches, to conclude a change of coach is required to get United out of the mess they find themselves in.

United have conceded 30 goals so far this season in 15 games - 19 in 10 Premier League matches, eight in four in the Champions League and three in their one Carabao Cup tie.

Aside from Pochettino, former Newcastle boss Eddie Howe, Italian Antonio Conte and former Germany boss Julian Nagelsmann have also been linked with the role.

Kieran McKenna was part of Ole Gunnar Solskjaer's coaching team at Manchester United and left Ipswich after four and a half years this summer. However, it is felt more likely United would want a candidate with greater experience than the 40-year-old Northern Irishman.

Instead of replacing Carrick another option under consideration is additional coaching support to assist the current team.

Bayern Munich coach Aaron Danks, who worked with Carrick at Middlesbrough and was touted as a potential appointment in the summer, is one option.

Manchester United co-chair Avram Glazer (left) with minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe at the 2025 Europa League final

If Ratcliffe was to decide otherwise, it would raise serious questions over the future of Berrada and Wilcox.

How could they work with Carrick again in that scenario?

The pair have been the subject of intense and frequent fan discontent. But sources are adamant that Ratcliffe still retains faith in the pair, even though United are heading towards sacking a manager in mid-season for the third successive year, having backed them in the summer and spend millions on new players.

Ratcliffe is a ruthless operator, and has clear opinions of his own. He also has form, spending £5m hiring Dan Ashworth as sporting director from Newcastle in 2024, then waiting for the 55-year-old to spend five months on gardening leave before he could start work.

Five months later, Ashworth was sacked due to a divergence of opinion over who should replace Ten Hag. Ashworth felt someone with Premier League experience was a better fit for United's squad. Ratcliffe wanted a more modern alternative. Berrada suggested Amorim. Wilcox, after initial reservations, also got on board. Amorim was dismissed after 14 months.

The other unknown element is the Glazer family. They will need to sign off any decision.

At the time of the Ratcliffe purchase, United confirmed the club's 'board' had handed over responsibility for the football side. But United's articles of association state that responsibilities delegated by directors can also be "revoked or altered".

Crucially, of the 12 current directors, six are members of the Glazer family, including co-chairs Joel and Avi Glazer. United's rules state that if required, the chairman of any meeting will have a second and casting vote.

Although there have been media reports of Glazer dissatisfaction at United's current plight, there has been no public statement on the matter.

Carrick won 12 games out of 17 as interim boss to earn a two-year contract as Manchester United head coach in the summer

It may seem strange, but the reality is, as with any employee, Carrick will continue to do his job until told otherwise - and so far, there has been no conversation to that effect.

Although most of his squad, and a significant number of academy players, are on international duty, a core remains at home.

This includes Mason Mount, Joshua Zirkzee and Matthijs de Ligt. Harry Maguire, who suffered a back spasm against Villa, is also there, as are other injured players, including Luke Shaw and Marcus Rashford.

Carrick gave his players a day off on Monday but scheduled training days for Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday. After that, they are not due to report back until 17 November, by which time the international contingent should start to return and begin preparations for the trip to Liverpool on 22 November.

"Obviously some of the boys will be flying off around the world and different things, and the group will be split for 10 days or so, but as a normal international week is, we'll have some training and we'll have one or two days off," Carrick said after the Villa game. "Not too much. But we'll train and get ready for the next game."

The victory comes after an 11-year legal battle by dual-citizen Jason Jones

A UK court has overturned laws criminalising same-sex intimacy in Trinidad and Tobago.

London's Judicial Committee of the Privy Council (JCPC), the Caribbean island's final court of appeal, ruled the laws were not in keeping with the "fundamental individual right to respect for private and family life."

The judgement is the result of an 11-year legal battle brought by dual-citizen Jason Jones, 62, who said he hoped it would "accelerate the fight for full equality."

Jones had successfully challenged the laws in 2018 in Trinidad's High Court, however the ruling was overturned on appeal by the Trinidadian government.

It is the first time the JCPC has ever decided on a case to decriminalise same-sex intimacy, and campaigners hope it will spark similar successful legal challenges elsewhere in the Commonwealth.

Prior to this historic decision, Trinidad and Tobago was one of some 34 Commonwealth countries continuing to criminalise homosexuality based on colonial-era British laws.

Under these laws, consensual same-sex intimacy is punishable by imprisonment, and in some cases carries the death penalty.

The Attorney General of Trinidad and Tobago had argued that the law was protected from legal challenges by the "savings law clauses" - which carried over existing British laws into newly independent states.

Representatives for Jones argued that the laws violated an individual's right to privacy and argued the government's changes to the laws in 1986 - which saw stricter punishments introduced - meant the savings clause protections no longer applied.

The judicial committee unanimously found in favour of Jones.

Handing down the judgement, Lord Sales told the court the laws "cannot be regarded as reasonably justifiable in a society that has a proper respect for the rights and freedoms of an individual".

Jones, human rights campaigner and appellant in the appeal, said: "These laws never reflected who we are as a people and a nation - diverse, multiracial, and secular.

"They told LGBTQ+ people that we were criminals in our own country. That message ends today."

Lawyer Anand Ramlogan SC, representing Jones, said the judgement was a "landmark victory for gay rights, equal dignity and respect for private and family life in Trinidad and Tobago."

As he prepares to reach a personal milestone, Brennan Johnson says he is happy with what he has achieved in football - but would like to reach more major tournaments with Wales.

The 25-year-old Everton forward is set to make his 50th appearance against Norway in the Nations League on Saturday, becoming the third-youngest Welshman to reach the landmark after Ethan Ampadu and Chris Gunter.

Johnson has one major tournament under his belt - the 2022 World Cup - having missed out on selection for Euro 2020.

Wales failed to make this summer's World Cup, but have huge incentive to qualify for Euro 2028 with Cardiff named as one of eight host cities.

"Even when I think about having a Euros here now, it is special," said Johnson.

"We've got a good squad and a lot of players playing at a good level. Everyone knows it's coming up and it motivates us to work hard and show what we can do."

Nottingham-born Johnson played for England at age-grade level before switching allegiances in 2018, a decision he has never regretted.

"As soon as I came to Wales I got a [good] feeling straight away and never looked back.

"You appreciate every cap for what it is, [50] kind of sneaks up on you a little bit.

"Playing at a World Cup was the highlight. It didn't go how we wanted it to, but I dreamed of playing at a World Cup from a young age.

Cerys Matthews received an OBE for services to music

Singer and presenter Cerys Matthews paid tribute to her family as she received an OBE.

Matthews, from Cardiff, was appointed an Officer of the Order of the British Empire (OBE) for services to music and received a medal from the Prince of Wales.

The 57-year-old hosts a BBC Radio 6 Music show every Sunday and was a founding member of Welsh rock band Catatonia who shot to fame during the "Cool Cymru" movement of the 1990s.

Speaking after the ceremony, Matthews said she accepted the OBE in memory of her family and "in gratitude of the freedoms I have as a female in this era".

Matthews' voice is also familiar to many over the Christmas holidays because of her 1999 rendition of Baby It's Cold Outside, sung with Sir Tom Jones.

Matthews' Catatonia shot to fame during the "Cool Cymru" movement in the 1990s

After the ceremony she said Prince William discussed Catatonia with her, adding he "evidently" was a fan.

Matthews wore Black Watch tartan - Scotland's royal regimental tartan - to the ceremony in memory of her grandfather Oswald, who served in World War Two and took part in the D-Day landings on the beaches of Normandy in 1944.

She said her grandmother, Olive, did not have the freedom to pursue music because of economic and societal barriers as a young, working-class wartime bride.

Matthews said Prince William was "evidently" a fan of Catatonia

"I grew up in the 80s and 90s as a female who loved music, and I've been allowed, and I've thrived, in the music industry.

"Sharing other people's music and making my own, and I accept this honour in their memory, and in gratitude of the freedoms I have as a female in this era.

"This positive change... I hope it continues across the world."

Meanwhile, techno DJ Carl Cox received an OBE for services to music after being a major figure in the British dance music scene for more than four decades.

Jeffrey Epstein died in a New York prison cell in 2019

Crimes committed by the late disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein after 2005 could have been prevented were it not for "failures" by federal investigators and prosecutors, a congressional investigation has concluded.

The Republican-led US House Oversight Committee on Tuesday released its final report into what it described as the "decades-long" mishandling of the criminal investigations into Epstein and his long-term associate Ghislaine Maxwell.

The report's findings are based on interviews and depositions with witnesses, government files, and financial records over a 15-month period.

Epstein died in 2019 as he awaited trial on sex trafficking charges.

"This is my way of trying to breathe," says Joanna Harris on speaking about Epstein for first time

"While some of these failures involved an exercise in poor judgement by the USAO, others appeared to be the result of Epstein's pervasive and wide-reaching influence," the report reads, referring to the US Attorney's Office.

It states that, rather than fully investigating allegations in other states, the USAO for the Southern District of Florida entered an agreement with Epstein in 2007 allowing him to evade federal prosecution.

'There is no justice' - Epstein survivor on how model agency sent her to abuser's home

Regarding Epstein's death in a New York prison , investigators concluded this was a result of "a series of institutional failures at the facility," which included staffing shortages, overworked employees, poor recordkeeping, and lax security practices.

Testimony the panel solicited was "unable to definitively dispel certain theories" surrounding Epstein's death, the report states, including accounting for a lapse in surveillance footage.

It found the justice department (DoJ) failed to communicate about document releases and that deficient redactions exposed survivors' sensitive personal information.

The DoJ has released millions of pages of Epstein-related files in response to legislation from Congress.

Earlier this year, the department had to remove thousands of documents related to Epstein from its website after victims said their identities had been compromised.

The report also alleges that financial institutions like American Express enabled human trafficking and immigration fraud, by allowing Epstein to use decoy flights and dummy itineraries to transport foreign workers across borders. The BBC has contacted American Express for comment.

The investigative panel recommended that Congress should pass legislation to prevent the weaponisation of non-disclosure agreements, which they said Epstein used to silence survivors.

"Epstein operated with impunity, shielded and enabled by powerful connections and a justice system that repeatedly failed his victims," said James Comer, the Republican chairman of the committee.

He called upon the DoJ to "interview or re-interview key witnesses, investigate Epstein associates accused of criminal activity, and ensure survivors have access to their records.

The department remains under bipartisan scruntiny regarding the Epstein files.

In the state of New Mexico, where Epstein had a ranch, the top state prosecutor accused the DoJ of stonewalling their criminal investigation.

"With all due respect, the Chairman's recommendations have already been addressed," a spokesperson for the department said in response to Comer's report.

"The Attorney General has repeatedly said that the Epstein case is not closed and there is no statute of limitations on human trafficking."

The report accuses Democrats of being "obsessed" with trying to implicate US President Donald Trump and that an "unfounded witch hunt continued without regard for the interests of survivors".

Trump has previously said he was friendly with Epstein before they fell out in 2004. The president's name has appeared thousands of times in the Epstein files but there is no suggestion that appearing in the documents implies any wrongdoing.

The committee's review of documents did not identify any that would implicate Trump, the report concluded.

In a statement, Rep Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the Oversight Committee, alleged his Republican colleagues "released a report based on an incomplete investigation and zero public hearings on Jeffrey Epstein".

Garcia accused the justice department of withholding "over 2.5 million pages of documents".

"We will not allow the President and his allies to dismiss this investigation," said Garcia, who is expected to lead the committee when Democrats take control of Congress in January following the recent midterm elections.

The family members of one of Epstein's most prominent accusers, the late Virginia Roberts Giuffre, thanked Comer for releasing Tuesday's report.

"A sentence from the report stands out to us: 'Questions remain as to whether the DOJ has released all its relevant documents.' We could not agree more and urge that all 7 million-plus files be released," Sky and Amanda Roberts said in a statement.

"There are many more individuals who have yet to be identified and brought to justice," they said.
