Meet the BBC Women's Footballer of the Year contenders

Voting is now open for the BBC World Service Women's Footballer of the Year 2026.

Fans worldwide can vote from the five-player shortlist of Temwa Chawinga, Ewa Pajor, Alexia Putellas, Alessia Russo and Khadija 'Bunny' Shaw.

The vote closes on Wednesday, 18 November at 09:00 GMT.

For the first time in the award's history, the winner will be announced as part of the BBC's Sports Personality of the Year on Sunday, 13 December as well as on the BBC World Service and the BBC Sport website and app.

Contenders for the award - now in its 12th year - are nominated by coaches, journalists and former professionals. It covers the period September 2025-August 2026.

Cast your vote, and read more on the five contenders.

Listen: Who is your BBC Women's Footballer of the Year 2026?

BBC Women's Footballer of the Year contender Temwa Chawinga

Chawinga has established herself as one of the world's most prolific forwards.

Her impact on the National Women's Soccer League is clear. Her extraordinary form helped Kansas City Current clinch the NWSL Shield as the league's top team in the regular season.

Chawinga scored 15 goals in the 2025 season as she became the first player to be named NWSL MVP in back-to-back campaigns. She also won the Golden Boot for the second year in a row.

Those performances earned her a contract extension through until 2029.

Chawinga returned to international football with Malawi for the 2026 Women's Africa Cup of Nations.

Alongside her sister Tabitha, she helped Malawi reach the country's first Wafcon final and - in doing so - qualify for the Women's World Cup for the first time.

Chawinga scored against Nigeria, Egypt, Ghana and Algeria at Wafcon, winning the tournament's Golden Boot with five goals.

BBC Women's Footballer of the Year contender Ewa Pajor

Pajor is widely regarded as a world-class number nine - and it's clear why.

Instrumental as Barcelona won four trophies last season, Pajor scored their first two goals in a 4-0 Champions League final victory over Lyon.

The goals meant she finished as the competition's top scorer, while the result meant she won the Champions League for the first time after losing in five finals - four with Wolfsburg and one with Barcelona.

Pajor also enjoyed an outstanding second season with Barcelona in Liga F, scoring 16 league goals in her 23 appearances and providing five assists. She was a key player as Barca won the domestic treble.

On the international stage, Pajor captains Poland and is the team's leading goalscorer.

BBC Women's Footballer of the Year contender Alexia Putellas

Club: London City Lionesses Position: Midfielder

Putellas showed again this year why she is one of the most influential footballers in the world.

After 14 years with Barcelona, she delivered a spectacular final season with the club - helping them win four major trophies.

Her 14 goal contributions in 11 Champions League appearances helped her childhood club win the competition for the fourth time, and she remained a decisive figure bringing experience and leadership when it mattered most.

Putellas delayed announcing her move to London City Lionesses to avoid creating a distraction, but in July 2026 she completed that transfer, saying the club's "women-only identity and ambition" were important factors.

Internationally, Putellas was instrumental in Spain retaining the Women's Nations League in late 2025, scoring three goals against Sweden in the semi-finals before being named player of the finals as Spain defeated Germany 3–0.

Last month she was awarded a record-equalling third Ballon d'Or.

BBC Women's Footballer of the Year contender Alessia Russo

Russo has proven to once again be a trusted and integral attacking force for Arsenal, while remaining a key player for England.

She scored 13 WSL goals last season to finish second in the league's scoring charts, and also added six assists in her 22 appearances. In total, she registered 24 goals and eight assists across all competitions.

Among the highlights of her season was winning the inaugural Women's Champions Cup with Arsenal, beating Corinthians 3- 2 after extra time.

It was the first competitive trophy Arsenal's women's team had lifted at the Emirates, though they finished runners-up to Manchester City in the WSL.

Russo remains a first-choice striker for England and in April scored her 30th senior international goal to move into the top 10 of Lionesses goalscorers.

She was also nominated for the PFA Player of the Year award.

BBC Women's Footballer of the Year contender Khadija Shaw

After a fine year, Shaw has positioned herself as one of the world's elite forwards.

The defining striker in Manchester City's Women Super League title-winning campaign, she scored 21 goals in 22 league appearances, won a record third consecutive WSL Golden Boot and was named WSL Player of the Season.

Her goals were central to City ending a 10-year wait for the league title.

They went on to complete the Double, with Shaw scoring the opening goal in their FA Cup final victory over Brighton at Wembley to finish the season with 26 goals in all competitions.

She also reached a major personal milestone in December 2025 when she became the first player in the history of City's professional women's team to score 100 goals.

Amid uncertainty over her future, Shaw announced at City's end-of-season celebrations that she had signed a new four-year contract through to 2030.

A delegation of 30 people had travelled to Oxford from India's Nagaland

The University of Oxford has returned the remains of 39 people taken from the Naga community during British colonial rule in India.

A delegation of around 30 people from Nagaland, a mountainous state in north-eastern India, attended a ceremony at Oxford's Pitt Rivers Museum on Monday to mark the handover.

The remains, most of which are skulls, will be taken back to India and given what Naga tribal leaders have described as a "respectful rest". There are plans to bury them under a joint memorial in a park in Nagaland.

Museum director Laura Van Broekhoven described it as "a historic moment that will be part of stories told to next generations".

She said the remains were finally on their way home after overcoming "so much red tape everywhere".

The human remains were displayed at the Oxford museum for decades before being removed from public view in 2020 as part of what it described as a "decolonisation process".

The museum formally handed over the remains and signed an agreement with Naga leaders on Monday

The Pitt Rivers Museum holds more than 6,000 objects associated with Naga culture, believed to be the largest such collection in the world. Most were acquired during British colonial rule in India and Myanmar (the former Burma).

The museum's website lists 219 items as human remains.

These were added to the museum's collection between 1910 and 1940 and mostly collected by two colonial administrators who were anthropologists.

The museum's website , external mentions that the objects collected during this period were "frequently confiscated during punitive military expeditions, rather than freely given".

During their visit to Oxford, the Naga delegation also met descendants of one of the anthropologists involved in collecting the remains.

"The manner in which these human remains were taken away from our land leaves much for us to speculate," one of the tribal leaders, Thejao Vihienuo, told AFP.

"I suspect that nobody would have given the skull of his father or his grandfather as a gift to another person."

Anthropologists say that the Naga people once practised head hunting, severing the heads of enemies as trophies. But they also kept the heads of their own chiefs at the centre of villages.

The Pitt Rivers Museum, founded in the 19th Century, has previously returned human remains to indigenous communities in Australia, New Zealand and the US.

The latest handover to India concerns only the 39 ancestral remains and comes after a visit by a Naga delegation to Oxford in 2025, when it formally requested their return.

The museum had announced in September that the remains would be returned to India.

Joan McConville started smoking as a student and became addicted

"To the day I die, I will regret putting a cigarette in my mouth".

These are the words of Joan McConville, who was first diagnosed with lung cancer in 2023.

The former teacher believes her cancer may have been caught earlier if screening had been available in Northern Ireland.

Despite growing evidence that early detection can significantly reduce death rates, Northern Ireland has yet to fund a targeted lung cancer screening programme.

Although the Department of Health previously committed to introducing screening by April 2027, it has now confirmed there was "no definitive timeline" for its full implementation because of funding.

Smoking is the biggest risk factor for lung cancer , external , although genetic and environmental factors can also contribute.

McConville, from Banbridge, started smoking at 19 while studying in Belfast and said she became addicted to nicotine.

"It's not that my generation didn't know the dangers of cancer. We did," she said.

"We started smoking because it was trendy. And I enjoyed it."

The mother-of-three tried "really hard" to stop smoking, particularly during her pregnancies, but "never succeeded completely".

She also struggled to quit after her diagnosis, despite being referred to a smoking cessation clinic.

The 71-year-old said she "was not remotely surprised" by her diagnosis, having smoked for almost 50 years and having a family history of cancer.

After several months of coughing - one of the symptoms of lung cancer , external - she was admitted to Craigavon Area Hospital (CAH) following a "dreadful coughing fit".

A scan to check for a clot revealed a 3cm (1in) lesion in her right lung. While surgery successfully removed the cancer, it returned earlier this year.

McConville initially had scans every six months but said more than a year had passed when she developed pain in the upper right side of her chest.

Initially dismissing it as an injury from gardening or housework, she said the "tiny little niggle" became increasingly severe along with "dreadful" nausea.

The symptoms eventually made it difficult to go into town, walk or visit her grandchildren.

Following another visit to CAH, further scans showed the cancer had returned and spread to her lymph nodes and ribs.

Surgery was no longer an option, but radiotherapy and chemotherapy were recommended.

McConville believes regular screening could have led to earlier treatment and surgery, potentially improving her outcome.

"If my cancer had developed between the ages of 50 and 70, which it did, then there's every possibility that it would have been found earlier," she said.

"I was a smoker. I probably would still have got cancer. If I could have had screening and it could have made a difference to me, that would make me angry."

She said many people underestimate the risks, believing lung cancer happens to others.

She said screening would have brought that message home.

"If it was pointed out at a very early stage to smokers like me, 'Look that tiny little dot is cancer. Stop smoking now and we'll hopefully be able to remove it and then that's it gone'," she added.

Respiratory consultant Wendy Anderson leads Northern Ireland's lung cancer network

Lung cancer remains the leading cause of cancer-related deaths in Northern Ireland, with about 1,370 people diagnosed each year, and more than a thousand deaths, according to Queen's University Belfast figures. , external

In 2022, the UK National Screening Committee recommended targeted screening , external across all four UK nations for people aged 55 to 74 who are at high risk of developing lung cancer, including current or ex-smokers.

Screening uses low-dose CT scans to identify lung cancer before symptoms develop.

England has begun rolling out screening, with full national coverage expected by 2030.

According to NHS England figures, nearly 13,000 lung cancers have been detected as a result with about three-quarters found at an early stage (stage 1 and 2) when cancer is most treatable.

Wales has announced a national programme , with the first invitations now expected in 2028.

While Scotland does not have a programme yet, it has been carrying out pilots , external .

Respiratory consultant Wendy Anderson leads Northern Ireland's lung cancer network.

She said while survival rates had been "increasing year on year, they're still not good".

"When I first started working as a consultant, less than one in 10 of our patients would have survived five years and now we're probably around one in four," she said.

Lung cancer is often diagnosed at a late stage where there are fewer treatment options available, meaning lower survival rates.

Anderson said screening could increase the proportion of people eligible for curative treatment from about 30% to 80%.

She estimated it could mean an additional 100 people a year surviving lung cancer or avoiding it altogether.

Screening could also tackle health inequalities by improving outcomes for people from more deprived communities, she added.

The respiratory consultant said reducing smoking rates remained the most important way to prevent lung cancer.

She added that stopping smoking not only reduced the chance of getting lung cancer, but also other respiratory diseases as well as heart attacks and strokes.

In December 2024, the former health minister Mike Nesbitt published a three-year health and social care plan , external to stabilise, reform and deliver services in Northern Ireland.

It said that "by April 2027, subject to additional funding, we will have a new targeted lung screening programme".

But now the Department of Health has said there is "no definitive timeline" for full implementation of the programme, as this will depend on future health funding.

It has funded a Public Health Agency (PHA) project team to assess what resources and funding are needed to deliver screening.

Planning will begin in December 2026 and is expected to take around a year.

Watch: Jensen Huang speaks to the BBC's Faisal Islam in 2025

Jensen Huang has the air of the late Steve Jobs about him. I have interviewed both, and the up-close charisma - and occasionally scratchy genius - is shared.

Both sported a signature item of black clothing, although Huang opts for a leather jacket rather than the Apple founder's turtle neck.

Both are innovators revered in the tech world. However, Huang is now being investigated over an affair with an alleged Chinese spy .

Everything you have heard about Artificial Intelligence (AI) over the past few months - good, bad, revolutionary and catastrophic - is dependent on having the most powerful frontier AI models.

In turn they depend on the most powerful microchips, and for years that has been this very company, Nvidia, led by Huang, and his technology rooted in repurposed games graphics and the manufacturing prowess of Taiwan.

Names such as Gracehopper, Vera and Rubin mean almost nothing to the public, but are the names of chips powering the creation of AI models transforming the world.

I met Huang as he held court with reporters and offered words of encouragement for the UK's tech future during US President Donald Trump's state visit to the UK in September last year.

It was also right in the middle of his attempts to get Trump to lift export bans to China of some of the highest performing AI chips, specifically the H200.

An export ban on a less powerful chip had already been lifted. He was, I suggested to him, one of the few people who could walk into the White House to meet Trump, and a few days later meet President Xi Jinping in Beijing.

He made no secret of his views, nor his assessment that he had persuaded Trump of his case.

"President Trump is very clear. He wants America to win and and President Xi wants China to win, and it's possible for both of them too. And the reason for that is because it's not a zero-sum game. The advance of human society is not a zero-sum game."

He is probably the only person in the world that could have spoken that sentence with the authority that he might have heard personally from both these superpower leaders.

However, his view about "zero-sum game" is not backed by many in national security circles.

Their view is that the race to the most advanced forms of AI is entirely zero sum, and requires the West - and the US in particular - to take critical action to hold back Chinese advancement.

The country that creates the most powerful AI systems, from the most powerful chips, will win, in terms of scientific development, of cracking encryption, economic growth and cyber-weapons.

He made a further argument: Far from being a national security challenge, it was, in fact, better for the US that the world "including China" became dependent on US systems, what they called the "American tech stack", with Nvidia chips at its core.

Huang then went even further than that, saying that President Trump "is very clear-eyed" about the idea that "this computing technology is not a national security concern".

He told me "any military is smart enough to build their military on top of their own indigenous technology, and not rely on an adversary to build their technology, build their military capability".

At that time, which is the same moment now being independently investigated over national security concerns and alleged Chinese espionage, Huang was making clear public arguments to lift export bans, and seemed to have a clear idea of President Trump's views.

More than that, he was also disputing the idea that his technology, in China's hands, was any type of national security concern.

Nvidia is the absolute epicentre of the AI tech boom in the US and of the global race for AI supremacy.

Even if the boom turned to bust, Nvidia is still expected to remain in rude health.

It has actual hard revenues of about $400bn this year. Monday's drop of about 4% of its value reflects new and extraordinary risks at this junction of tech and global politics, but the chipmaker is still worth more than $4 trillion.

Ian Kirke struggled to watch his side's FA Cup first round match against Altrincham due to thick fog

For many football fans, an FA Cup win is the stuff of dreams. But for 690 Notts County supporters, thick fog meant they could barely see it happen.

Ian Kirke was among the Magpies fans whose view of Saturday's FA Cup first-round tie against Altrincham was obscured by fog, leaving many unable to see the League One side's penalty shootout victory.

The thick layer of fog provided chaos not just for the players and fans, but also commentators and camera operators at the J Davidson Stadium.

Kirke said fans had to rely on the cheers - or silence - from the home support during the shootout. "It's the most bonkers festival of football I've ever seen in my life," he added.

Heavy fog meant Notts County fans were unable to watch the penalty shootout that took place at the other end of the pitch

Lifelong fan Kirke, who lives in Berkshire, said the weather at kick-off was "like any normal match".

Before fog descended over Greater Manchester, Jacob Bedeau had given Notts County the lead just before the half-hour mark.

The hosts, who play in the National League, hit back as Lucas Weaver and Lewis Banks scored to give Altrincham a 2-1 lead.

With the conditions worsening, referee David Rock opted to continue with the tie, which saw the camera often unable to pick up the ball.

The referee's decision to continue the game paid off for Notts County, who levelled the tie at 2-2, when Callum Roberts scored from the edge of the box.

"It's like a fever dream" - commentators struggle through fog

"I can just about see the bright white numbers on their shirts, but I am struggling to see what is happening on the far side of the pitch," said BBC Radio Nottingham commentator Adam Hassell.

Former Notts County striker Mark Stallard was also commentating on BBC Radio Nottingham, and said: "We're looking around, and here in the press box no-one knows where the ball is! It's like a spot the ball competition.

"We genuinely cannot see the linesman or the players on the far side. It's slightly farcical having to commentate for radio listeners."

Lynda Lally said the fog got worse during the second half

Fellow Magpies fan Lynda Lally, from Beeston in Nottinghamshire, said the weather got "worse and worse" after half-time.

"For the other 45 minutes, we could only see what was happening once players emerged from the fog," she said.

The weather became "a cross between an eerie Christmas nativity gone horribly wrong - and the 1980s film called The Fog," Kirke said.

Kirke added the fog that led to an FA Cup third-round replay between Notts County and Wimbledon being abandoned in 2001 "wasn't as bad" as it was at Altrincham.

"I don't know what on earth had to happen for the referee to call it off," he said.

With the game going to penalties, Lally had hoped the shootout would take place in front of the Notts County fans so she could finally see the ball.

"Once we found out it wasn't, we were thinking what is going to happen because we can't see anything," she said.

"There was a deathly silence amongst the Notts fans when Altrincham fans at the other end were excited, and when they went silent, we went wild."

Kirke said his friend, who was struggling to see the action on TV, texted him updates during the penalty shootout.

"The only way we could ascertain what was going on was the reaction of the Altrincham fans," he said.

The sound of disappointment echoed around the stadium as Altrincham missed the target three times, before Rosaire Longelo slotted home the decisive penalty to seal a 3-2 shootout victory for Notts County.

"We heard the silence and we went into a massive roar knowing we had won," Lally added.

Thousands gathered at Krakow's historic Market Square to honour the victims of Saturday's attack

Thousands of people joined a silent march through central Krakow on Monday night, in memory of those killed and injured when a gunman went on a violent rampage at the weekend.

The crowd were led by Poland's president and prime minister, the bitter political rivals putting on a rare show of unity after the country's deadliest attack in modern times.

As they reached the historic Market Square, a bugler played from the tower.

Many people were carrying flowers or candles to leave at the shrines that now dot the cobblestones, each one marking a spot where someone died.

Fiercely proud of its reputation for safety, Poland has been profoundly shaken by this attack. It has left people struggling to make some kind of sense of what happened.

The alleged gunman has been named as 24-year-old Michal Oksinski by local media.

Critically injured in a shoot-out with police, he did not regain consciousness and died in hospital early on Monday .

Initially, the interior minister claimed that Oksinski was driven by far-right, extremist views. The national prosecutor's office now says that it is too soon to say he was "inspired" by any ideology.

"The minister wanted to win domestic political points. That's not responsible behaviour," Pawel Musialek of the Jagiellonian University suggests, in a country where politics is highly - and often viciously - polarised.

"So far we've seen no clear message that this guy was strongly ideological, and that it's not more like something from the darknet."

There has been no mention of any letter or manifesto that Oksinski left. One neighbour told Polish news site Onet that the 24-year-old was a "bit of a loner" but few who knew him well have spoken publicly.

What we know so far after Krakow gun attack

In addition to his electronic devices like his phone, investigators are examining a number of badges that Oksinski had attached to his military-style outfit.

The prosecutor's office says a yellow Gadsden flag with a coiled snake symbol was displayed in his bedroom. "It has various meanings of freedom and rebellion," a spokesman emphasised. "Not necessarily negative."

It was at Oksinski's home that the bodies of his parents and sister were discovered.

It is alleged that he shot them, before driving some 200km (125 miles) south to continue the killing in Krakow.

Candles and flowers have been placed around the square in places where someone died

Two days on, shops and cafes around the market square are beginning to fill up again, but the mood is subdued.

A Zara clothes shop is still boarded up, after bullets smashed the glass. A local man in his 50s died just outside.

Jo, a Scottish tourist, saw paramedics "who got there ridiculously fast", fighting to save him. "It was all pretty grim."

Like many, she initially mistook the rifle shots for fireworks.

On the opposite corner of the square, beside another cluster of flowers, people keep pausing to take pictures of the holes that were blasted into the wall by gunfire.

One of the six victims has been identified as a Polish painter in her 50s, who was a mother of four, and in town with friends for an exhibition opening.

A British citizen and an Austrian who died are yet to be named publicly.

Several drivers of the horse-drawn carriages that are usually poised to trot tourists around the square were seriously injured.

Olha, a Ukrainian citizen, moved to Krakow for safety when Russia launched its full-scale invasion

Olha, who works in a nearby chocolate shop says everyone is now nervous.

On Saturday, people rushed into her store to escape the gunman who was tearing around in his car, firing through the window.

Olha is Ukrainian, and moved to Krakow when Russia invaded. "We left our own country for safety. This is supposed to be a safe place!" she said.

"It's so sad, and so scary. Especially that he drove all the way here for two hours, planning this and thinking about it."

She regrets that the gunman did not survive: "So many are dead, so many lives have been ruined, and now there will be no justice."

Political differences were set aside between President Karol Nawrocki (left) and Prime Minister Donald Tusk (right) at the vigil on Monday

When Oksinski's car was searched, four firearms and "hundreds of rounds of ammunition" were found, all owned legally by the alleged killer and his father.

Both were members of the Swit Starachowice sports club, where there is a shooting range. A spokesman recalls Michal Oksinski as unremarkable: average competition results and normal behaviour.

He had been just three times this year, most recently in August with his father. The club spokesman is adamant that it does not train combat firing, only shooting from a fixed point.

Gun ownership in Poland has grown considerably since war broke out in Ukraine just across the border, but this is the first mass shooting anyone here can remember.

Inevitably, it has brought scrutiny of the checks over who qualifies to handle such weapons, including psychological tests, as Michal Oksinski passed all of them.

On Monday, the government announced an urgent review.

"Thank you Mr Policemen, get better soon"

At the spot where Oksinski's car was intercepted and he was shot by police there is another memorial, this one in honour of the officers still in hospital.

Some have brought flowers, but a girl called Bianka has left a card that reads: "Thank you Mr Policemen, get better soon."

A couple of steps away, there's a series of bullet holes in the glass.

"This man was a real hero, he didn't hesitate," Ania says, referring to officer Jakub Kulik who was shot in the chest. His condition remains serious. "We're here to help him fight for his life."

"Nothing like this has never happened before, it's terrible," a young man called Wojtek tells me.

He's only glad that the gunman responsible for such horror turned out to be Polish.

"People here are already against immigration, so that would have been even worse."

Ania thinks Poles will pull through, though the country's image as a low-crime oasis has been shattered.

Most of all, she's angry that Michal Oksinski died without being held to account for the devastation.

PM Anthony Albanese says the law needs to catch up with a "fast-changing world"

Australia plans to create a new AI safety regulator and has flagged criminal penalties for tech companies who do not comply, months after an OpenAI hack.

In September, Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese revealed that a rogue OpenAI agent had "infiltrated" a government health website and other systems, and criticised the company for taking months to tell them about the hack.

On Tuesday, he released the 18 recommendations made after a "rapid review" into the breaches including new safety and security standards for AI companies such as mandatory reporting of hacks.

AI brings opportunities, he said, but Australia must prepare for the "new risks" from this "rapidly advancing technology".

"The law needs to get ahead of and, in some cases, make sure that it catches up with, what is a very fast changing world," Albanese said.

One of the recommendations suggests changes to criminal law to have a standalone "failure to prevent" offence .

This would criminalise instances where a company develops "an AI model that engages in harmful conduct" and "fails to take reasonable steps to prevent that harm".

The review also recommended "mandatory, time-bound AI safety reporting" of hacks.

This point addresses what Albanese had earlier called his "disappointment" in the months-long delay for OpenAI to tell his government about the breach.

In June, a statistics portal containing "non-sensitive" data from Australia's universal healthcare scheme Medicare was hacked by a rogue OpenAI agent .

OpenAI said it only learnt of the breach in August while reviewing "misaligned model activity" and emailed a general inbox of an Australian government agency on 10 September.

It took several more days before the email was escalated to Australia's cybersecurity centre, with a message then sent to a government minister ahead of the prime minister being told.

Albanese said he spoke to OpenAI boss Sam Altman and raised "Australia's extreme concern about this incident", with Altman acknowledging there were "issues with protocols" at OpenAI.

Days after the hacks were revealed, OpenAI delayed its rollout of a new AI model, citing safety concerns.

Yongeye avuga ko amahirwe y’uko Amerika yosubira kugaba ibitero kuri Iran ari make cane, naho ashimangira ko ingabo zayo ziteguriye kwishura mu gihe ibintu vyohinduka. Trump yanse gutangaza ku mugaragaro ko intambara yarangiye, avuga ko ibihugu vy’incuti za Amerika biri mu Kigobe c’Abarabu bishobora kubandanya bihura n’iterabwoba riva muri Iran. Imbere y’aho kuri uwo munsi nyene, Trump yari yakiriye muri Maison Blanche umushikiranganji wa mbere wa Qatar, Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdul Rahman Al Thani. Impande zompi zavuze ko ibiganiro vyabo ku bijanye no kurangiza intambara vyagenze neza. Mu kiganiro aheruka kugira kuri televiziyo, yavuze ko ata mpamvu abona yotuma intambara yongerekana. Iyo ntambara kandi yarateje impari za poritike i Washington. Umushingamateka w’Umurepubulikani Thomas Massie yasavye ko umushikiranganji w’ukwivuna abansi Pete Hegseth abogozwa, nubwo Trump yamushigikiye avuga ko ibi bifise intumbero za poritike. Abademokarate bavuga ko bashobora kubandanya n’uno mugambi mu gihe inama nshingamateka na nkenguzamateka nshasha zizoba zitanguye ibikorwa vyazo. Wrexham are competing in the Championship for the second consecutive season under Phil Parkinson

With 15 games of the Championship season gone, Wrexham have steadied the ship.

Phil Parkinson's side responded to a run of three defeats in four matches by claiming four points from their home double header with promotion-hopefuls Middlesbrough and Wolverhampton Wanderers.

It ensured they entered the final international window of 2026 in positive spirits.

As the club action takes a two-week break, BBC Sport Wales looks at the highs and lows of the Red Dragons' season to date.

So how does Wrexham's performance so far this term compare to the same stage last season?

Wrexham's performances in the draws with Cardiff City and Watford early on were encouraging.

They made light work of dispatching strugglers Preston North End and have earned highly-impressive wins against top sides including Millwall, Southampton and Middlesbrough.

Defensively, Wrexham's expected goals (xG) faced of 18.17 is the fourth-best in the division.

They have also made just one error leading to a goal, the joint-best return alongside four other teams in the Championship.

Up front, Kieffer Moore - who scored 13 times for the Red Dragons in all competitions last season - has netted five goals so far this term, in addition to claiming two assists.

The Wales international's return comes from an xG figure of just 3.23, meaning he has outperformed his xG by 1.77. He has also won 68 aerial duels, with only four players in the league managing more.

Others such as Jacques Ekomie, Issa Kabore, Ben Whiteman, Joe Worrall and Callum O'Hare have shown real glimpses of settling in after joining on permanent deals in the summer.

Amid the increasing noise surrounding the club's struggles earlier on, Parkinson yet again demonstrated an impressive ability to remain grounded and get his side back on track.

In terms of the league standings, Wrexham sit six points adrift of the Championship play-off places and eight clear of the relegation zone.

So there is plenty of reason for the Wrexham faithful to remain optimistic.

When it comes to the numbers, only five teams have a lower xG total than Wrexham's figure of 16.80, while only three sides have managed fewer than their 50 shots on target.

Wrexham's four through balls made is - alongside Lincoln City - the joint-lowest in the division.

Home defeats by Birmingham City and West Bromwich Albion were particularly underwhelming, while the 6-0 thrashing at West Ham United represented a real low point.

Following the 2-0 loss to Blackburn Rovers in October , former Wales international Nathan Blake suggested Wrexham were losing their "fear factor" and that they were in danger of becoming "ordinary".

The Red Dragons then produced a lacklustre display as they were beaten 1-0 by Sheffield United.

It promoted a strong response from Parkinson who said he and his players would not shy away from any criticism.

After the draw with Wolves, midfielder Lewis O'Brien said of the post-Blades debrief: "I think we had to look at ourselves, deep down. It was a tough couple of days."

On the back of the 1-1 draw with Wolves , which came three days after an impressive 2-0 win over Boro, Parkinson declared his side had needed a reboot following the defeat by the Blades.

"We've had a bit of a reset this week in terms of what the performances need to look like for our supporters and everybody at the club," said the manager.

"We know we've got the capabilities to win games, but like everybody, you can easily have a capability to lose a game and you've got to be right at it.

"There's no 80% scenario in this division, everybody's got to be at it, focused and ready, and we really were ready in these two games. We can take a lot of credit from that."

Injuries certainly have not helped the club's cause, while there have been several off-the-field issues too.

The Red Dragons have been fined twice fielding ineligible players.

Chief executive officer Michael Williamson departed last week, with Shaun Harvey taking over as acting CEO.

It has clearly impacted the club's efforts in the opening third of the season.

"You always have things going on in football clubs, it's never smooth running anywhere," Parkinson said after the Wolves draw.

"But I think this has been particularly disjointed, for various reasons."

Ben Sheaf, Max Cleworth and George Thomason have all returned to action in recent weeks following significant spells on the sidelines through injury.

Nathan Broadhead is also closing in on a return, although it remains to be seen when last season's top scorer Josh Windass, Callum O'Hare and Liberato Cacace will be available.

Discussing the November international window, Parkinson said: "It's a chance to get some work in the lads who need to work and build on what we've done this week."

Unfortunately, Sam Smith is set to miss the remainder of the season and will undergo surgery this week after sustaining a serious knee injury at Sheffield United.

It will likely prompt the Red Dragons to scour the transfer market for an additional frontman in January given that Bailey Cadamarteri is the only other option behind first choice striker Moore.

Davis Keillor-Dunn could also potentially be recalled from his season-long loan spell at League One side Sheffield Wednesday - where he has scored five times in 11 appearances.

But the outlook on the campaign overall has certainly improved in the past week.

Wrexham fans hope more progress can be made over the coming months.

California voters have voted to reject a wealth tax on its billionaires.

The ballot proposal would have levied a one-time tax on the state's mega wealthy to help fund healthcare. It took nearly a week of counting votes after the midterm election to determine a projection on the measure.

There are about 200 billionaires in the state, including Meta's Mark Zuckerberg , reality television star Kim Kardashian and media mogul Oprah Winfrey.

Proposition 40 targeted Californians with a wealth of more than $1.1bn (£800m) with a 5% tax on their total wealth, including assets such as shares as well as income. It failed amid divisions among Democrats and labour unions.

Are California voters about to impose 'world's first' tax on billionaires?

Had it passed, experts believe it would have been the world's first wealth tax targeting billionaires.

The tax would have raised about $100bn to make up for federal funding cuts to healthcare in California as a result of President Donald Trump's sweeping tax and spending bill.

Those who backed the measure had argued it would help ensure that the ultra-wealthy were contributing their fair share and helping backfill gaps in the state's budget.

The wealth tax faced fierce opposition, including from Google co-founder Sergey Brin, as well as California Governor Gavin Newsom and labour unions.

Newsom, whose tenure as governor is coming to an end, had expressed concerns that the measure could cause the wealthy to leave the state and drive out their crucial income tax revenue.

Some billionaire critics of the measure spent millions trying to crush it, with a handful even moving out of the state to evade the possible tax. Brin gave more than $100m to a political organisation funding ballot measures that could block the tax, according to the Los Angeles Times.

Dave Regan, head of the union that led the charge for the measure, said on election night that the billionaires' efforts to block the tax created "a lot of confusion and a lot of second-guessing among people who really in their hearts know what the right the thing to do is".

Regan, who is president of Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, pledged to seek a billionaire tax once more in 2028.

The measure had odds stacked against it, with two other propositions on the ballot that would have effectively reversed it, even if it passed.

California, home to some 23 million registered voters, has the largest economy in the country and boasts the fourth largest global economy. It is home to one of the highest concentrations of billionaires in the world, but also has one of the highest wealth gaps.

MN202611_1ptmhjzfe0t.t:
Jemima Goldsmith (left) and Russell Brand (right) dated for about a year in the mid-2010s

Warning - this report contains graphic content.

Jemima Goldsmith, the ex-girlfriend of Russell Brand, has accused him of "violence, coercive control and abuse" while the two were together.

Goldsmith, who dated the disgraced entertainer for roughly a year around 2014, alleged that she "had to call the police to have him removed from my house in 2014 during a violent incident" but chose not to press charges.

In a lengthy statement on social media, the 52-year-old said she was "in awe of the courageous women who came forward at Brand's trial" and was "glad and relieved" he had "finally faced justice".

Brand, 51, was sentenced to 10-and-a-half years in prison earlier on Monday after being convicted of rape and sexual assault.

He was found guilty of raping a woman at his home in 2009, as well as three counts of sexual assault against three other women.

The judge at the sentencing hearing told Brand that he harboured a "casual arrogant disregard to any woman's right to say no to you", while his fame meant he believed "you could act when you liked and how you liked".

How the outspoken comedian went from Hollywood stardom to a prison sentence.

Russell Brand sentenced to 10-and-a-half years in prison for rape and sexual assault

TV producer Goldsmith is also the former wife of ex-Pakistani prime minister and cricketer Imran Khan, the daughter of late billionaire entrepreneur Sir James Goldsmith and sister of ex-Conservative government minister Zac Goldsmith.

The mother-of-two said she had chosen not to pursue legal recourse against Brand over the alleged violent incident in 2014 as she was "worried about the impact of the press attention on my then teenage children".

She wrote on X on Monday evening: "Whilst my pain in relation to this pales in comparison to what the women have testified in court have suffered, this was a difficult period in my life which has had a lasting impact."

Goldsmith said she had not seen nor spoken to Brand since 2014, but claimed to have assisted the journalists who exposed the allegations against him and had been willing to testify to his "abusiveness" were they sued.

In her statement, she also addressed reports of an injunction taken out by her and Brand in October 2015 that banned a woman, Szilvia Berki, from harassing them including by making allegations of assault by Brand at Goldsmith's home the prior year.

Goldsmith said on Monday that Berki had visited her house for roughly 30 minutes on 7 June 2014 to give Brand a massage, which she said did not end up taking place once she arrived.

Jemima Goldsmith (pictured) alleged she once had to call the police on Brand

Goldsmith said that Berki later told police that Brand had pushed her in the back while she had been leaving and that she had been attacked by Goldsmith's dog. Brand's ex-girlfriend said she "did not see anything untoward" during the encounter.

She added that, after providing a statement and CCTV footage, police concluded that there was no case to answer.

Goldsmith accused Berki of then sending a series of "vicious antisemitic and threatening" messages and posting "wild and untrue allegations" about her on social media.

She said she then agreed to a suggestion from Brand's lawyer to seek an injunction to prevent harassment. She claimed on Monday that recent media reporting of the injunction had opened her up "to vile hatred and abuse online".

Sunday Times chief news correspondent Rosamund Urwin, who was involved in a media investigation into Brand in 2023, has told the BBC that Goldsmith helped her "a lot".

"I have seen the abuse she's been getting online and I did try to tell people that part of the story was much more complicated than they realise," Urwin said.

"I wish people would remember women that come forward are brave people and that is what she has done tonight – she has spoken out with immense bravery about how Russell Brand treated her," she added.

How the outspoken comedian went from Hollywood stardom to a prison sentence.

Watch: Moment judge sentences Russell Brand in court

Watch: How rapist Brand was never far from controversy

Brand's sentencing hearing heard victim impact statements from the women he had been accused of assaulting.

One of them said she was "upset and traumatised" for years after the incident, adding: "I didn't have any respect for myself. I was thinking I was damaged goods - scared of giving off signals that could be taken the wrong way."

The woman he was found guilty of raping said the trauma was something she had to "carry every day".

A van believed to be carrying Brand was seen arriving at HMP Wandsworth in London on Monday after the sentencing hearing.

The guidelines state offenders jailed for four years or more for some serious violent or sexual offences will be released at the two-thirds point. In Brand's case, that would be seven years.

Once released, he is likely to spend the rest of his sentence on licence and will have to abide by specific rules such as wearing a tag.

The disgraced entertainer was found guilty of the charges involving four women between 2004 and 2009 following a four-week trial at Southwark Crown Court.

He was found not guilty of two counts of rape and one count of attempted indecent assault.

MN202611_himzj4fvzy.t:
Trump: "Iran militarily is effectively over"

Donald Trump has said "Iran militarily is effectively over", and said that there is "positive momentum" behind negotiations to end the Middle East conflict.

"We're just keeping it the status quo," the US president said on Monday. "And we're doing that really at the behest of countries that are their neighbours."

Trump's comments came after he met the Qatari prime minister. Qatar is a US ally in the Gulf region, and one of Iran's neighbours, which has been a key mediator in efforts to end the war.

Addressing reporters in the White House press briefing room, Trump said that renewed US attacks on Iran were "highly unlikely" but that the US was "locked and loaded" should the circumstances change.

Iranian officials have repeatedly expressed doubts about Trump's prior comments about resolving the conflict.

This is not the first time that Trump has said the Iran war is "militarily" over, but the circumstances for him are different now.

The president has hinted at de-escalation in Iran after a bruising set of midterm election results for the Republicans last week, which senior figures including Vice-President JD Vance blamed on the Iran war.

Ahead of the midterms, Trump had said US forces conducted what he described as "minor strikes" on an Iranian island in the Strait of Hormuz . However, in an interview with 60 Minutes that aired on Sunday, the president said that he did not currently see "any reason" to escalate the conflict.

Responding to a question over why he would not officially declare an end to the war, Trump said that some of the Gulf allies could still face Iranian aggression.

"We have some great allies there and we have to make sure they're not hurt," he said, suggesting that the US naval blockade on Iranian ports was helping to make the region more secure.

Global oil prices, which have fallen sharply since the midterms, dipped further after Trump's comments.

On Tuesday afternoon in Asia, Brent crude was more than 1% lower at $91.50 (£52) while US-traded was down by 1.2% at $85.82.

Could Democrats in Congress end the war in Iran?

Trump hosted Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdul Rahman Al Thani in the Oval Office earlier on Monday, saying they had an "excellent conversation" about negotiations to end the war.

In a post on X, the Qatari leader said he held "positive discussions" with Trump and Vance on "reaching a deal and bringing peace to the region".

Efforts to broker a peace between Washington and Tehran have largely been held indirectly through mediators since the war first broke out following joint US-Israeli strikes in February.

Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates are among the US's Gulf allies that have been hit by Iranian strikes over the course of the war, in addition to the threat of strikes that have led to major air travel disruptions in the region.

Republican congressman Thomas Massie plans to force a vote in the House of Representatives this week to impeach Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth

Post-election recriminations over the US war in Iran are already placing pressure on members of the Trump administration.

Republican congressman Thomas Massie launched a strong attack against Trump's Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth on Monday over the war in Iran, requesting a vote in the House of Representatives to impeach him.

Trump has backed Hegseth, who says he is "not worried" about the looming impeachment threats, calling Massie's effort a "sham".

While the move is unlikely to succeed with Republicans still in control of Congress until January, Democrats have expressed willingness to impeach Hegseth once the new session begins and they have control of both the House and the Senate.

MN202611_6p70l1zx1v.t:
Qantas CEO Vanessa Hudson apologised for the "hard news" of 850 job cuts

Qantas will outsource 850 local corporate jobs to consulting giant Accenture with most roles moving to India as the airline fast-tracks AI investment.

In an internal email to staff on Tuesday, the Australian company's CEO Vanessa Hudson said "this is hard news for some and I'm sorry for the uncertainty it brings".

The job cuts will begin mid-2027, she said, and start with finance, procurement, people and marketing roles shifting "mostly" to teams in India and "some in Australia" as the firm seeks to modernise its IT systems.

Hudson said the "scale and speed of change in technology and AI is something none of us has seen in our lifetime", and it was in talks with unions and staff on the plans.

The move comes days after the airline provided a market update, flagging fare increases and flight cuts amid higher fuel costs.

On its new multi-year deal with Accenture, Hudson said it was about "modernising" the airline's IT systems to become "more efficient".

Qantas spends more than AU$1bn (US$691m; £514m) a year on technology, she said, and the company's back-end systems needed to be upgraded.

"Like every airline, we run on technology built up over decades for a different era, including more than 1,000 legacy applications that were never designed to work together," she said.

The deal with Accenture means "we will redesign and simplify parts of how our corporate functions work and reduce duplication", Hudson said, so staff can "spend more time on work that creates value for our customers and the business".

The company said that "in time", the work that Accenture takes over will be "transformed further with automation and AI".

Staff affected by the job cuts will be redeployed "where possible", the firm added, including new roles in Australia.

Qantas - which employs about 28,000 staff in Australia and another 4,000 globally - said thousands of its staff already use AI in their daily work.

The BBC has contacted the Australian Services Union for comment.

MN202611_1ynh1g29xww.t:
The arrest comes weeks after the cruise came to a sudden end, leaving 200 guests stranded in Cambodia

A round-the-world cruise that left passengers stranded in Cambodia after its US-based operator ran out of money has been seized in Singapore.

The Odyssey, which set off from Belfast in October 2024 and was meant to take guests on a years-long voyage around the world, is now anchored in Singapore port waters, local authorities say.

Around 200 guests were forced to leave the ship last month in the Cambodian port city of Sihanoukville, after its owner Villa Vie Residences abruptly suspended operations citing "extraordinary increases in fuel costs".

The crew onboard are reported to be well, Singapore's port authority said.

"Arrangements for their welfare and wellbeing are being managed by the vessel's creditors," the authority said, adding that the vessel had been "placed under arrest pursuant to a court order".

Singapore law firm Helmsman LLC has been named the "arresting solicitor", but it is not clear which party it represents.

The Odyssey was meant to go on a three-and-a-half-years voyage covering 150 countries.

Passengers were given the options of buying their cabin outright, which allows them to stay onboard beyond its initial voyage, paying for a five-year residency, or renting a cabin for days-long tours.

Permanent residencies in its cabins ranged from $120,000 (£89,272) to $440,000. Those cabins were also available for rent from $3,500 a month, according to its website.

"For roughly the price of a car, you can own your home on a ship that travels the world," its founder Mikael Petterson had earlier said.

However the cruise was beset with problems from the start, with its departure delayed for four months because of repairs and paperwork.

While in Vietnam, crew members reportedly bought food from local grocery stores because the company owed money to a vendor who refused to deliver food, according to CBS News, the BBC's partner in the US.

CBS also reported that the operator warned passengers of its financial troubles in August, when it had sailed on a separate occasion into Singapore, and had to raise money from guests to keep the cruise going.

It had also mentioned the risk of being detained then.

Holly Hennessey, one of the ship's passengers, had earlier told the BBC guests were asked to consider paying a fuel surcharge as prices soared, and that their itinerary had been "severely curtailed".

The vessel sailed again into Singapore earlier this month, weeks after the cruise came to a sudden end while in Cambodia.

As the Iran war sent fuel prices soaring earlier this year, monthly fuel cost per cabin in parts of Asia had risen to as much as $8,000 from $1,800, Villa Vie Residences said in a statement on 27 October.

It added that it had taken "significant steps to reduce fuel consumption" but those measures turned out to be insufficient to offset the "extraordinary increase in fuel costs".

The company also said it was working with residents to "identify temporary living arrangements" while in Cambodia.

MN202611_p4zujjsr0d.t:
Mali Osmalek says she was stuck in a cycle of automated responses from Vinted

Mali Osmelak never imagined that selling clothes on Vinted would end with a court claim to recover almost £6,000.

She started trading on the platform to earn an income while managing Crohn's disease and caring for her four-year-old daughter.

But when she became a professional seller in March, she was unable to complete Vinted's verification process, leaving thousands of pounds inaccessible in her Vinted wallet. After several weeks of trying to resolve the issue, Mali took legal action.

Vinted says sellers may be asked to complete verification checks to comply with legal and regulatory requirements and 98% of transactions are completed smoothly without needing help from its support team.

Vinted is hugely popular in the UK with 17 million users. The online marketplace does not charge a fee to sellers for listing on there.

After the BBC reported on users whose accounts had been suspended or banned , dozens of people got in touch describing difficulties accessing money held in their Vinted wallets.

Mali joined Vinted in 2024 as a side-hustle. Demand for her second-hand gymwear grew rapidly and, within months, she had set up a limited company to expand the business.

This year she signed up for a Vinted Pro seller account - designed for people who want to sell a high volume of items and who are registered as a business.

Within weeks she had generated almost £6,000 in sales. But when she tried to withdraw the money, she discovered her account had been restricted and was told she needed to complete a verification process.

"I thought, 'That's OK. It's not rocket science,'" she says. "I'd set up the business with the help of an accountant and had all the information they needed."

Mali says she spotted an error Vinted had made with her name and she flagged it with Vinted, but "again nothing was done and the verification kept failing". She found herself stuck in a cycle of automated responses.

In an effort to break the deadlock, she also contacted Mangopay, the payments company that at the time operated Vinted sellers' wallets and processed transactions on the platform. She was directed back to Vinted.

After eight weeks without access to the money, Mali decided to take both companies to the small claims court, spending £455 in court fees.

Three days after the court claim was filed, Mali says the account was "magically verified" and she could withdraw the funds.

She still pressed ahead with the case though to try to recover her court fees, costs and interest.

In June, she obtained a default judgement after neither Vinted nor Mangopay responded to her claim, with the court ordering the companies to pay £1,207.50.

But she has yet to receive the money. She has since been informed that Vinted and Mangopay have applied to have the judgement set aside, with a hearing scheduled for December.

"It's been ridiculous and incredibly stressful," she says.

"I need that cash. I will fight it. I'm going to tell the court their system is completely broken. I needed help and nobody helped me."

Vinted said: "Ms Osmelak's check was not successful because her documents did not match the name on her Vinted account. We have since helped her update it, and her account is now verified."

The company did not respond to the BBC's questions about the legal action Mali has taken and continues to pursue.

Mangopay said it was "bound to professional secrecy and data protection obligations. We are, therefore, not allowed to comment on individual cases involving our clients or their users, nor can we share details about specific accounts, transactions or legal matters."

Azri Mukthar says he has now stopped selling on Vinted

Sportswear seller Azri Mukthar told the BBC he has been trying to withdraw almost £2,500 from his account for over a year.

The businessman was more than happy to become a Pro seller as he was already registered as a limited company.

"I submitted all the documentation they requested and got the go-ahead from Vinted. So then I uploaded all the products and got 30 to 40 sales immediately," he says.

But when he wanted to withdraw his earnings, he found that he couldn't.

"They said my verification was pending," he says.

Azri shared a frustrated conversation he had with Vinted's AI assistant

Azri too, says he's been round in endless circles repeatedly submitting documents only to get an immediate response saying they had been rejected.

"It's frustrating and annoying as there's no clear system to follow.

"You contact customer support and they say you've not submitted X, Y or Z. But I know I have done all they're asking for."

He claims a certificate from Companies House that Vinted requested has been declined 15 times.

Azri has now stopped selling on Vinted and says he is going to have to start legal action.

Vinted said: "Mr Mukthar's check could not be completed because he did not provide all the required documents. Our support team is currently in touch with him to help with his verification."

MN202611_acn2qwfz7q.t:
Roza has decided to share her story with the BBC

A woman raped by Jeffrey Epstein says the president of the model agency representing her put her in danger, when he sent her to two photoshoots at the convicted sex offender's Florida beach house.

At the time, in 2009, Epstein was serving a jail sentence for sex offences against a minor but was allowed to work each day from his home.

"My agency's job was to protect me, and they failed. In fact, they put me in danger. And for that, they should be held accountable," she tells the BBC World Service.

Roza was 18 when she was first sent to Epstein's Palm Beach home by MC2 Model Management's US branch, having only arrived in the US from Uzbekistan about a month earlier. MC2's US president at the time, Jeff Fuller, now runs another US model agency called The Source Models.

"My agency knew exactly where I was. So Jeff knew exactly where I was going," says Roza.

Jeff Fuller now runs The Source Models agency

She shows us an expense statement suggesting Fuller himself booked her flight home from Palm Beach, following her second shoot at Epstein's home. Fuller has previously claimed he did not know Roza was going to Epstein's house.

She says the photoshoots led to her being employed as an assistant to Epstein. Other survivors have explained how the financier used the recruitment of assistants as an elaborate ruse to allow him to continue abusing young women .

Roza says Epstein went on to systematically rape her.

Fuller has not responded to the BBC's allegations. He has previously said he did not know Roza was being abused.

We discovered through the Epstein-related documents released by the US Department of Justice [DOJ] that 10 models from MC2 met, or were in communication with, Epstein after his conviction.

The files also show Epstein gave $1m (£742,000) to MC2 in 2005 - despite the agency owners telling a US publication two years later that Epstein had no involvement in their company.

Testimony shared with BBC Eye also raises questions about the role played by two other individuals who were active in the model industry, and whom the DOJ files show had close relationships with Epstein - former agent Ramsey Elkholy and agency director Faith Kates.

A DOJ statement from last year, that no evidence has been uncovered which would warrant further investigation against "uncharged third parties", is now being challenged by New York State senator, Zellnor Myrie.

He has proposed a new sex trafficking bill to give police greater power to investigate Epstein's alleged enablers.

Senator Myrie told the BBC he wants those who knew - or should have known - about Epstein's abuse to be held accountable

Sara Ziff, founder of the Model Alliance, which campaigns for stronger protections for models in the US, approves.

"Often, [model agencies] are the problem. They are the link between the model and these predatory men."

Roza says the person behind the camera at the photoshoots MC2 sent her to was not a professional photographer, but Epstein's girlfriend at the time, Nadia Marcinko .

Roza describes the set-up as "strange - there was no stylist" and the photos were never used. She has since become convinced the shoots were stage-managed by Epstein and MC2.

BBC Eye reveals new evidence showing how scouts, agencies and powerful fashion figures helped Jeffrey Epstein gain access to young women after his conviction for sex offences.

If you are outside the UK, please watch on YouTube , external

An email in the DOJ files, from Fuller to Epstein, makes clear the close ties between the agency and the financier.

"Had it not been for you, we would have fired her months ago," Fuller writes of another model in March 2012. "And I would be careful as she blabs about things," he says.

A month after Epstein's second arrest in 2019, MC2's US branch was dissolved and Fuller opened a new agency, The Source Models, which is still operating. The BBC has found that 50 models from MC2 were transferred to his new agency.

We asked The Source Models to comment on our findings - it did not reply.

Model agencies were useful to Epstein, says Sigrid McCawley, the lead lawyer for more than 100 of Epstein's victims.

"Epstein said to many people he wanted three different girls a day. Think about those numbers... The [model] scouts were really critical because they were the ones who were identifying the type of woman that Epstein liked."

In the case of former agent Ramsey Elkholy, BBC Eye has discovered he tried to connect 34 women to Epstein, including an 18-year-old who was still in school.

The experience of one of the women highlights how assistants would be co-opted into the structure of the abuse.

Elkholy, the DOJ files show, suggested to Epstein that one of the financier's female assistants befriend this woman, before introducing her to Epstein.

We spoke to this woman, and she revealed that at her first meeting with Epstein, aged 19, he sexually abused her in his New York townhouse.

Ramsey Elkholy told the BBC: "I completely reject any allegation that I knew of or facilitated abuse of any kind… At the time, I had no knowledge of any abuse and I knew only his own [Epstein's] account of his 2008 [legal] case, which I misguidedly believed."

He continued: "The record and published reporting show that women were often groomed by other women in his inner circle. I was never part of that circle, or indeed of any such activity… my intention was to help models find professional opportunities by introducing them to an extremely well-connected individual."

If you are in the UK and you have been affected by any of the issues in this story such as sexual abuse and violence , information and support is available at BBC Action Line

Lawyer Sigrid McCawley says these female assistants would have had "no choice" in how they conducted themselves.

"These young survivors were being abused regularly. Their livelihoods were being threatened… They had to do what they were being told to do."

Another model we have spoken to, Simona (not her real name), from eastern Europe, told us Epstein had raped her more than 200 times.

"People think that we gained something, that we agreed on this abuse in order to gain something, whether it's monetary or influential, but it's not true. We're left with deep trauma," says Simona.

She says the first time she met the financier, aged 20, she was already signed with a model agency in New York, and he offered to introduce her to his "good" friend Faith Kates.

At the time, Kates was the head of Next Management, one of the world's biggest model agencies. She stepped down from that senior executive position in December last year, but is still legally listed as a director of the company.

Simona says Faith Kates, pictured here, met her at Epstein's request

Simona says at this meeting, Kates suggested she undergo plastic surgery and sent details of a surgeon to Epstein.

After her meeting with Kates, Simona says Epstein convinced her to stop modelling.

And just like Roza, and several other of his victims, she became his assistant. She says he went on to rape her and control every aspect of her life for nearly two years.

The DOJ files show Epstein asked Kates to meet an additional five models, though it is not clear how many of these meetings took place.

Lawyers for Faith Kates told the BBC: "Jeffrey Epstein was a master manipulator... Ms Kates was one of those grossly misled by Epstein. Had she known then what she - and everyone else - now knows, she would have never associated with him."

They added she had never asked a model to have plastic surgery.

We approached Next Management for comment, but it did not reply.

Myrie told the BBC that if his bill were to become law, and "you were sending models to Epstein and you knew what Epstein was doing, or you should have known what he was doing, you will be held accountable".

Roza says at the moment, "there's no justice for me, nothing's going to make everything go away".

But she hopes sharing her story will encourage others to come forward.

"There are many, many survivors out there who never speak, because it's scary. So to all my sister survivors… you know me now. You know my name. I say, reach out."

MN202611_1b88vbb1rs5.t:
Senior officials from Ukraine, Russia and the US will reconvene for a second day of talks on Wednesday

The first of two days of trilateral talks between Ukraine, Russia and the US aimed at ending the war in Ukraine has concluded in Abu Dhabi.

While senior officials from Kyiv and Moscow were tight-lipped after the four hour-long discussions, President Volodymyr Zelensky, who was not at the talks, said they had proved "constructive and quite substantive".

Speaking from Paris, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio also said the meeting had been "very productive".

Although expectations for a breakthrough that ends Russia's full-scale war on Ukraine are low, US officials said earlier that Moscow and Kyiv were privately showing "a little bit of flexibility" on the issue of who would control Ukraine's eastern regions in a postwar scenario.

Zelensky also said that humanitarian issues such as prisoner of war exchanges had been discussed.

At the start of Tuesday's talks President Donald Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, told delegates that the US had "narrowed the gaps" between the two sides, without providing details, and hoped to move towards a "solution that hopefully ends the war".

Kushner had said earlier the talks would be focused on addressing the "postwar security concerns" of both Russia and Ukraine.

Asked later at a news conference in Copenhagen about the approach of US officials to negotiations, Zelensky said: "I see changes. I'm very happy with what I hear."

Kushner and Trump peace envoy Steve Witkoff also met Ukrainian and European and Nato officials on the sidelines of the main meeting.

European leaders have pushed to be included in the discussions amid concerns that decisions about their continent's security would be made without them.

The Americans appear to support this, with Rubio acknowledging during a visit to Paris that the Europeans "are a part of solving this problem for the long term".

However, "the Russians have a bad taste in their mouth with the Europeans", according to a US official.

Some proposals favoured by EU officials - such as calling an unconditional ceasefire as a prerequisite for peace negotiations - are routinely rejected by Moscow. Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said on Tuesday that a truce would just allow Kyiv to regroup. "We will not agree to it," he said.

Moscow and Kyiv's positions are still far apart on ending the conflict.

A key area of disagreement involves Ukraine's eastern region of Donetsk, which is mostly occupied by Russia.

Moscow has demanded that Ukraine relinquish the parts of Donetsk it still holds, while Kyiv wants to freeze the contact line to maintain control over those areas, which it says are crucial to its future security.

While neither side has budged on these demands, the US official speaking on the eve of the talks suggested that this was just the public stance and that Moscow and Kyiv had shown "a little bit of flexibility, privately".

However, he acknowledged the issue would not be solved without discussions about a new "security architecture".

"They will not solve the Donetsk issue and the territorial issue until they know what the security architecture is going to be after the war," the official said. "And keep in mind, we're not going to be able to finalise one without the other."

For Ukraine, a post-war "security architecture" may include reassurance that allies will come to its aid if it comes under attack again. For Russia, that could be its longstanding ambition to see Nato roll back from Eastern Europe – which would be alarming to Europeans.

The framework being proposed includes security consultations and crisis communications hotlines, as well as "reciprocal de-escalation measures" between the two. The officials also floated the re-activation of the Nato-Russia Council that has been largely paused since 2022.

Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff are part of the US delegation that will attend the talks in Abu Dhabi

The last round of trilateral talks, held in Geneva in February, ended without a breakthrough. Soon after, the US-Israel war on Iran diverted Washington's attention from Ukraine, and no other discussions were held since.

From the start of his second term in office, US President Donald Trump – who once boasted he could end the war in Ukraine within a day – has spearheaded several rounds of talks to end the conflict, albeit with little success.

Meanwhile, his increasingly conciliatory approach towards Moscow has fuelled deep unease in Kyiv and across the European Union.

After meeting Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev in Washington last week, Trump touted a forthcoming "big, beautiful agreement" on Ukraine that "might involve all of Europe".

Many in Ukraine are sceptical that this would result in a fair peace.

Ukrainian MP Oleksandr Merezhko, head of the foreign affairs parliamentary committee, told the BBC he believed Trump wanted "a quick deal at the expense of Ukraine", which will certainly be rejected by Kyiv.

The only way to make Russia's Vladimir Putin start real negotiations was by putting greater pressure on Russia through sanctions and deep strikes, Merezhko said.

"While Putin has a war machine up and running, he has no incentives to negotiate." He also mentioned recent moves by Trump, such as his deal to buy diesel from Russia, as something that "only encourages Moscow to continue the war".

Moscow's delegation in Abu Dhabi includes Kremlin aide Vladimir Medinsky, deputy foreign ministers Sergei Ryabkov and Mikhail Galuzin, spy chief Igor Kostyukov and army general Yury Zhigarlovsky.

Kyiv has sent several senior officials who have been part of previous negotiating teams, including Foreign Intelligence Service head Rustem Umerov, Volodymyr Zelensky's chief of staff Kyrylo Budanov, and MP Davyd Arakhamiya.

Away from Abu Dhabi, Russia continues to pummel Ukraine with deadly bombardments and strikes on energy infrastructure, viewed in Kyiv as proof that Moscow wants to corner Ukraine into accepting a deal on Russia's terms.

On Monday, Kushner was cautious to point out that the Abu Dhabi talks could at most "build momentum toward the next phase of negotiations".

"This is an extraordinarily difficult and complicated conflict," he wrote on X, adding the US was "approaching these discussions with determination and realism."
